full_text:
"I have to go with this day to day,” Tua Tagovailoa said of the Falcons' starting QB job. “What I can control is how I prepare, how I play, how I perform.” Kevin C. Cox / Getty Images
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. — On Sunday, Tua Tagovailoa will join a club that is bigger than it probably should be.
He will become the 14th quarterback to start a game under first-year Atlanta coach Kevin Stefanski when the Falcons face the Steelers in Pittsburgh.
In six years in Cleveland, Stefanski started 13 quarterbacks in a regular-season game — Baker Mayfield, Case Keenum, Nick Mullens, Jacoby Brissett, Deshaun Watson, Joe Flacco, P.J. Walker, Dorian Thompson-Robinson, Jeff Driskel, Jameis Winston, Bailey Zappe, Shedeur Sanders and Dillon Gabriel. Averaging more than two starters per season is a tough way to live in the NFL, said Norv Turner, who was the offensive coordinator in Minnesota for three seasons while Stefanski was an offensive assistant with the Vikings.
“The No. 1 thing you have to get right is the quarterback position,” Turner said. “The things they did in Cleveland (at the position) set them back so much and made it a real difficult coaching situation. If you get the quarterback thing right, then the coaching becomes a lot easier.”
Time will tell if Tagovailoa is the right option for the Falcons. He was signed to a one-year, $1.2 million free-agent deal this offseason after being released by Miami, where he spent six seasons and left the Dolphins with a dead-cap hit of nearly $100 million.
“I would say it’s a blessing,” Tagovailoa said Wednesday of his second chance in Atlanta. “It’s not something that I take for granted.”
It will be Tagovailoa’s 77th career regular-season start and his first since Week 15 last season, which also came against the Steelers in Pittsburgh. He was 22-of-28 for 253 yards and threw for two touchdowns and one interception in that game, which was played in 17-degree temperatures. He was also sacked four times. He was replaced by rookie Quinn Ewers after that game and did not play another snap for the Dolphins.
“When something gets taken away from you, you start to think about all the things you could have changed,” Tagovailoa said. “Looking back at my time in Miami, there are things I could have done better. There’s a lot of things I think I could have done better, turning the ball over, could have played better, my decision-making … it just wasn’t good enough.”
Tagovailoa is getting the start in Week 1 over Michael Penix Jr., who said earlier this week that he still doesn’t feel ready for game action while recovering from a torn ACL suffered in Week 15 last year. Penix was cleared for 11-on-11 practice work on Aug. 24 and said he feels “real close” to being ready to play in a game.
“How I am taking it is, I have to go with this day to day,” Tagovailoa said of the starting job. “What I can control is how I prepare, how I play, how I perform.”
Veteran Cooper Rush will serve as Tagovailoa’s backup against the Steelers, while Penix will be inactive. The Falcons will tailor their game plan to Tagovailoa’s strengths, Stefanski said. In six years in Miami, the quarterback was fourth in the NFL in completion percentage (68 percent) but 50th in air yards per target (7.4). In the last two seasons, Tagovailoa’s air yards per target dropped to 6.3, which ranks 63rd in the league in that span, according to TruMedia.
“Any coach, you’re worth your salt if you’re doing what your players do best and leaning into what your players do best,” Stefanski said. “Quarterbacks are comfortable with certain things, and they are not comfortable with everything. Our job is to figure out, ‘What in this broad scheme fits his eye?’”
The Falcons have been searching for an answer at quarterback since Matt Ryan, who is now their president of football, started all 16 games of the 2020 season. Five quarterbacks — Marcus Mariota, Desmond Ridder, Taylor Heinicke, Kirk Cousins and Penix — have made at least four regular-season starts since then. Running back Bijan Robinson has played behind four of them in his three seasons in the league.
“I just make sure I am here to support them no matter what,” Robinson said of playing with a new starter at the position. “My job is to make sure they are supported when I talk to the media so they can feel confident going into it.”
Robinson has followed that plan with Tagovailoa throughout the preseason.
“He has a lot of talent around him, and I think it’s going to make him a lot more confident,” Robinson said. “It’s just him having that trust in us to put the ball in our hands.”
That game plan will feature plenty of Atlanta’s rushing attack, Robinson believes.
“There’s a desire by a lot of coaches to show everything you’ve been working on, and that’s just not reality. There are just not enough plays for that,” Stefanski said. “For Tua and all of our players, understanding what the game plan entails, understanding what we are trying to attack on each play is the most important thing.”

full_text:
Jesse Minter's era as the Ravens' new head coach will begin Sunday in Indianapolis. Mitch Stringer / Imagn Images
OWINGS MILLS, Md. — Jesse Minter and Declan Doyle had a lot to do.
As the new head coach, Minter was busy building his Baltimore Ravens staff, implementing a defense, getting familiar with an organization he had been away from for five years and embracing every aspect of a move across the country to start a dream job .
Hired to run Minter’s offense, Doyle had only been in Baltimore for a couple of days. He barely had time to move into his new office, never mind laying out all the plans for establishing and teaching an offensive scheme.
All of those things could wait. They had a message to deliver to Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson, and they felt it needed to be done in person.
Months later, that early February trip to South Florida to spend a few hours with Jackson resonates more for what the two coaches heard and observed than what they said.
“I knew Lamar, had talked to him on the phone a few times. He was involved in the interview process,” Minter said. “I knew he was excited about something different, but I wanted him to really be excited about Declan and the direction of the offense. We came away from that meeting like, ‘Wow, this dude is all in. He’s really excited.’
“He told me right then that he was going to be there for a lot of the offseason program. That was the first thing he told me, without me even bringing it up.”
Minter and Doyle said plenty, too. They wanted to make sure Jackson understood they viewed this as a partnership, and Jackson was the reason they were so excited about their new roles.
“Both of us honestly wanted the job because of him,” Minter said.
In many ways, that meeting on Jackson’s turf between the two-time league MVP coming off his most challenging season, the first-time 43-year-old head coach and the 30-year-old first-time play caller set the tone for the season. The Ravens get things underway Sunday afternoon in Indianapolis.
For Minter, a longtime defensive assistant and coordinator, Sunday is a culmination of a rapid rise since he left Baltimore following the 2020 season. He was one of the most coveted head-coaching candidates in this cycle after two strong years of leading the Los Angeles Chargers’ defense. But the Ravens’ job, vacated by the abrupt firing of one of his mentors, John Harbaugh, was at the top of his list.
For Jackson, this is his ninth season, yet it hasn’t felt that way as he prepares. It will start with the ongoing questions about the 29-year-old’s future in Baltimore — his contract expires after the 2027 season — and his adaptability to Doyle’s offense.
“I feel like I’m a rookie or a second-year guy,” Jackson said earlier this week. “It’s not about the new system or the new coaches or anything like that. The past is the past, and you can’t dwell on that. I’m focused on what’s going on right now. I’m just excited to get back out there and start the season off better than we did last year.
“I want to win (Sunday) and focus on winning a whole lot more games this season, and hopefully that gets us to the promised land.”
It’s been a successful walk-up for Minter’s Ravens. The players have embraced his understated, workmanlike approach. They spent the summer raving about Minter and the new staff’s attention to detail and structure. The good vibes were evident from the start of the offseason program, and they haven’t relented.
The player buy-in is exemplified by the star quarterback, who has spoken boldly about the offense’s potential , responded to Doyle’s hard coaching and put in the work on the field and in meeting rooms.
“I think it was important for him to express to us that, ‘Hey, I’m bought in, I’m ready to go and I’m excited about what’s new,'” Doyle said. “You only can go as fast and as far as your operators. Those positions are trigger points, and he’s certainly one of those. He was hungry to learn it, and it really hasn’t changed all the way up until now.”
There’s been a lot of time over the past several months spent dissecting what led to the end of Harbaugh’s successful 18-season tenure . It’s a topic team officials and some veterans have grown weary of. However, one thing that’s undeniable, even for Harbaugh’s most vocal defenders, is that change can be necessary. It creates a different energy, too.
Minter has ridden that wave while staying true to himself and his coaching principles. After a coaching search that featured more than 20 interviews, he understood he wasn’t hired to build a team culture from scratch or to scrap everything his predecessor established. The Minter touch has been more subtle.
His practices started earlier but were a little shorter and less frenetic. He chose season-long captains rather than selecting them weekly. He focused on the details and situational football. Within the facility, he’s spent as much time as possible with different players and position groups, all while getting the defense ready as its play caller.
“I think I’m pretty good as a multitasker myself, but watching Jesse bounce around like he does is really super impressive,” general manager Eric DeCosta said. “At one point — because my office is over here, and his office is right there — I would be going over there to see him, and he’s never in his office. Because Jesse is coaching defense. He is always with the defense.”
There would be preseason practices where Minter’s voice didn’t rise above the din of a typical training camp workout. Veteran defensive lineman Calais Campbell described Minter’s coaching style as “matter of fact.” Cornerback Keyon Martin said coaching moments with Minter were more of a conversation than a lecture. But when something needed to be said, Minter got straight to the point.
“I’ve been very impressed and surprised at how he’s kind of progressed throughout the years,” said veteran cornerback Marlon Humphrey, who had Minter as one of his position coaches earlier in his Ravens career. “When you come from, obviously, Harbaugh (was a) very alpha-type, leader-type guy. I was interested to see how different team meetings would be. It’s been really good how Jesse has addressed the room and how he’s addressed just small situations.”
Humphrey recalled a moment early in training camp where the defensive backs were debating a coverage question. In the very next meeting, Minter addressed it immediately, outlining how it would be done.
Minter has been a part of successful defenses pretty much everywhere he’s been, so his hiring was accompanied by an expectation that he would help fix the Ravens’ defense. The questions mostly revolved around how he would lead the entire team. The Arkansas native is not prone to fiery speeches or outbursts. He operates on an even keel. He’s never going to be the “win the news conference” or “create a headline” type.
Ravens defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver had a seven-year playing career and is now in his 17th year as a coach. He said Minter is the most “personable and normal” head coach he’s ever been around.
Minter, however, showed this summer he’s not afraid to let his guard down. At a team dinner during road joint practices with the Minnesota Vikings, Minter took the microphone and belted out the lyrics of Eminem’s “Lose Yourself.” The players went wild.
“I didn’t feel like I had to go in there and try to prove, ‘Oh, I have to try and be this way that I’m not really (like),'” Minter said. “They know me. They wanted me to be myself. It’s definitely made it really comfortable — not comfortable in a sense that it’s going to be easy, but comfortable in a sense of, I can just operate and be myself, get the thing rolling the way I wanted to, have freedom to feel like I can change things that I want to change.
“But also I have a ton of respect for the way it’s been done here forever, beyond who the coaches were. There’s a cool understanding of how the organization has been built and also them wanting a fresh look at certain…

full_text:
The pressure on Brandon Beane to deliver a Super Bowl championship intensified after the Bills fired coach Sean McDermott and promoted their longtime GM. Timothy T. Ludwig / Getty Images
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. — Brandon Beane sits in a black leather chair, facing the windows where the old Highmark Stadium once stood tall. All that remains now is rubble and memories of the last nine years of Beane’s life.
Going from “The Ralph” to the new $2.2 billion stadium across the street is fitting in a lot of ways, especially this season. A lot has changed with the Bills between 2017 and today. Almost everything, in fact.
Everything, that is, except for Beane.
The Bills general manager, who added the title of president of football operations this offseason, looked at a photo from one of his first pre-draft news conferences in Buffalo.
“Holy s—, that’s crazy,” Beane said. “Obviously a lot less gray hair back then.”
Beane enters the upper echelon of stability among GMs in the NFL by hitting his 10th season in 2026. He is one of 10 current GMs who have hit double digits, one of only nine who don’t double as their team’s owner.
Beane’s tenure is rare by previous Bills franchise standards. He is one of only two GMs to reach 10 years, the other being Bob Lustig, who served as the Bills GM from 1967 to 1978. Beane has to make it to 2029 to top Lustig.
“That’s hard in this league to win as much as they have,” Giants GM Joe Schoen said. “Every year, your roster’s in a different situation, your salary cap’s in a different situation. You have coaching changes and everything else, and just, to me, to watch him be able to maintain that has been impressive.”
Lustig was the Bills GM for only nine seasons after the NFL merger. Beane has 45 more regular-season wins than Lustig and more than doubled Lustig’s win percentage (.321).
Overall, Beane boasts more regular-season wins (98) and a higher winning percentage (.662) than any Bills GM before him. The Bills are currently in the longest stretch of consecutive winning seasons (7) in franchise history.
Despite the regular-season success, the ultimate prize eludes the Beane-led Bills. Former Bills GMs Bill Polian and John Butler had shorter tenures and fewer regular-season wins, but both reached the Super Bowl.
Reaching and winning a Super Bowl. Those are the very things that keep Beane up at night, phone on full blast, ready to take any call that comes his way.
That pursuit led to a split once difficult to imagine: The Bills fired coach Sean McDermott , ending his nearly decade-long partnership in Buffalo with fellow Carolina Panthers alumnus Beane.
It’s put even more focus — both inside and outside the building — on the Bills to reward their once-in-a-generation quarterback, Josh Allen, with the only thing his surefire Hall of Fame career doesn’t have.
How has Beane lasted longer than any other Bills GM in nearly five decades, and what has he learned along the way?
What toll has the scrutiny taken on him and his family, particularly after McDermott’s firing?
And how does he keep it all together?
Years before Beane became the Bills GM, he and his wife, Hayley, took their sons, Tyson and Wes, to Disney World. They were in a long queue for Test Track.
“Brandon has this habit of when somebody says their name, he repeats it so he can remember it. And if they’re wearing a name tag, watch out because he’s gonna say it a million times,” Hayley recalled. “One of the linekeepers is walking by, and he sees the name tag. I don’t even remember what (the name) was. But he’s just like, ‘Oh, hey, Sally, how are you doing?’ And he’s just striking up a conversation, and (our sons) are like, ‘Oh my God.’ They’re mortified. And he’s like, ‘Yeah, we’re just standing in this long line. You don’t got any shortcuts, do you?’ And she’s like, ‘I don’t think so.'”
Beane explained later that Disney workers are probably used to getting yelled at during the day. His counter with kindness worked.
“Five or 10 minutes later, she comes back to us after they had a chat, and she was like, ‘Psst, come here,'” Hayley said. “She takes us, and this backdoor opens, and we literally walked right onto the ride. He turns around, he’s like, ‘Boys, it’s all about building relationships.'”
Past roster building and managing the salary cap, that lesson to his sons is the central pillar that keeps Beane in such high regard around the building.
Players, coaches, agents and staff at every level — Beane has a rapport with everyone. Most who come into contact with Beane rave about him as a boss and communicator.
“I’ve always been about relationships, but I think it’s as important to me today as it ever has been,” Beane said. “You’re going to go through ups and downs in this business, and you need to be able to have strong relationships in your organization, and that’s at all levels. Because if you don’t, that’s where the cracks in the foundation can happen and cause turmoil.”
His mother set the example. A frequent volunteer, she would stop to greet acquaintances during grocery trips after church, prompting his father to tease her about needing to speak to everyone she knew. To her, it was simply the right thing to do.
Beane carries that lesson into his work, believing that making time for people ultimately benefits the organization.
Hayley and Brandon have been married since they were 22, and both just celebrated their 50th birthday. When they met at UNC Wilmington, Beane’s initial life plan was to be an English teacher and a high school football coach. The NFL came later.
Hayley has seen Brandon’s entire NFL trajectory, from when he started off making $5.15 an hour as an intern for the Panthers to becoming Bills GM. That includes being on the clock, around the clock.
“The reason I deal with it and I put up with it is because he’s so ridiculously happy and he has found his true passion in life,” she said. “How many people truly can say they get up every morning and go to work and they love what they do?”
But beyond time on task, the job’s frustrations often bleed into the times Beane isn’t technically working.
“Honestly, I just try to listen,” she said. “And if I can help at all, offer suggestions or offer a different viewpoint to where… you’re thinking about it with the NFL brain, take it back from a family or a wife or a kid or something and think about things from different perspectives.”
“She’s a rock star with just her patience with this job,” Beane said.
The Bills were starved for success when Beane arrived in May 2017. And it was quite the first 12 months.
Beane traded five players during his first training camp, another before the 2017 trade deadline and two more ahead of the 2018 NFL Draft.
Armed with draft capital, Beane’s next deal was easily his defining moment, sending out Nos. 12, 53 and 56 to move up to No. 7 for Allen.
The moniker “Big Baller Beane” was universally adopted. His approval ratings stayed sky-high for years, especially with Allen’s leap to stardom in 2020. In 2022, The Athletic ’s Bills fan survey yielded a 94.9 percent confidence rating in the GM.
From there, though, it began to wane.
After signing Von Miller to a massive free-agent deal, the Bills were Super Bowl favorites in 2022, opening with a statement win over the Los Angeles Rams. The early returns were undone when Miller tore his ACL on Thanksgiving. Then on Jan. 2, the NFL world stopped when Damar Hamlin suffered cardiac arrest and collapsed on the field before having to be resuscitated.
“That’s the one year I can say, like, I don’t think our team had a chance anymore,” Beane recalled. “It was hitting guys at different times, at different levels. It was emotional, it was draining, and different things like that. We came out and won the game the next week. It wasn’t perfect, but it was just not the same after that.”
The Bills squeaked by a Skylar Thompson-led Miami Dolphins team in the Wild Card round that season. The following week, they fell to the Cincinnati Bengals at home.

full_text:
The Texans sacked Josh Allen eight times in last season’s 23-19 win, dropping the Bills quarterback to 0-4 in Houston, including the playoffs. Alex Slitz / Getty Images
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. – Deer season in Texas begins next month for bowhunters, in November for everybody else.
Josh Allen season will be held Sunday in Reliant Stadium.
Can the Houston Texans bag him again?
“They got after us last year,” the Buffalo Bills’ franchise quarterback said. “There’s no secret about it.”
Buffalo is trying to reestablish itself as the AFC team to catch. Its five-year division title streak was snapped. Sean McDermott was fired.
Now first-year head coach Joe Brady will make his debut in a locale where Allen never has won and against a hungry foe.
“Their defense is easily the top defense in the NFL in my opinion,” Bills right tackle Spencer Brown said, “the way they fly around and really chase the ball, the secondary, how they cover, and they got $80 million tied up in pass-rush guys.”
The Texans went big-game hunting last year and couldn’t have been more thrilled in a 23-19 victory.
Houston took Allen down for eight sacks, hit him four other times and pressured him on 44 percent of his pass attempts despite mostly sending just four defenders. He threw two interceptions. Brown and left tackle Dion Dawkins suffered injuries that sidelined them the next game, too.
Edge rushers Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter combined for 12 tackles, 4 1/2 sacks, six quarterback hits and a pass breakup. On one Anderson sack late in the first quarter, Allen kicked his feet in agony and later revealed the hit made his left arm go numb. Two other Texans defenders recorded two tackles for losses apiece.
“We just had the energy all week long,” Anderson said after the game, “like, ‘Man, we’ve got to go hunt. We’ve got to be relentless. No matter what you got going on, no matter how you feeling, bro, there’s no weak links out there on the field. You want a piece of the gazelle? You’ve got to go hunt for the gazelle.’”
Buffalo is expecting no safer environment this time, either. Houston’s defense might be better this year.
The Texans return a core of eight starters for a third straight season. Cornerbacks Derek Stingley Jr. and Kamari Lassiter and nickelback Jalen Pitre are perhaps the NFL’s top trio. The Texans added Philadelphia Eagles free-agent safety Reed Blankenship (to play alongside Calen Bullock) and three-time Pro Bowl edge rusher Jadeveon Clowney.
Buffalo will have its hands full.
“That might be my least favorite thing to see is Josh on the ground,” Bills tight end and captain Dawson Knox said, “especially when you’re blocking the guy that tackled him, but that is extra motivation. We want to keep him clean. We want to say there was zero sacks throughout the game, but also it’s just the nature of the NFL. Those guys are incredible as well.”
The Texans’ defense was so dominant last year that it didn’t need much help. Journeyman backup quarterback Davis Mills started for the injured C.J. Stroud. Mills’ competency was enough – even as Bills running back James Cook ran 17 times for 116 yards and a touchdown.
Allen has played some of his worst games in Houston. In four games there, Allen has completed 53 percent of his passes for 732 yards and one touchdown with two interceptions, two fumbles and 14 sacks.
“Every game has its own flow, got your own situations that you’ve got to handle and take care of,” Allen said. “They’ve had some really good defenses in the past, and it’s no different now.
“But, obviously, I want to go out there and want to play the best that I can play and want to help our team win a football game. That’s all that it comes down to, whether it’s me completing 30 balls or handing it off 40 times. Whatever it takes for us to win this game is what I’m willing to do. They’re going to make it tough for us.”
The Bills can find solace in how they responded to last year’s savagery.
One week later, with Alec Anderson and Ryan Van Demark starting at tackle for Brown and Dawkins, the offensive line blanked Pittsburgh Steelers demons T.J. Watt, Nick Herbig, Cameron Heyward and Alex Highsmith. Allen was hit once, sacked zero times in a 26-7 victory.
The Bills that night showed the previous week in Houston wasn’t them.
“We’re going to be the Buffalo Bills,” said Anderson, now the starting left guard. “We’re going to do what we want, whether that be run the ball or pass the ball. We might just choose to run the f— out of the ball.
“That will define our season, that we have our Weapon-X, and that’s Josh Allen, but you don’t want to use your weapon every single play. Why not use another weapon like James Cook? It will be a great year to really put an entire offense together.”
Buffalo added receiver DJ Moore this offseason, and for last year’s trip to Houston the Bills didn’t have tight end Dalton Kincaid, who was hurt. The injury report looks encouraging for the opener, with only running back Ty Johnson and defensive back Jordan Hancock not practicing Wednesday.
The extra offensive help will be welcome as Allen tries to conquer what has been an unbeatable host.
The Bills are trying not to put too much emphasis, though, on not turning the season opener into open season.
“I’m sure if we lose, ‘The season’s over; the Bills are a bust,’” Brown said. “And I’m sure if we win, ‘We’re going to the Super Bowl,’ and our Super Bowl odds go up to plus-5000.”

full_text:
Newcomer Cam Lewis acknowledges he hasn't yet mastered Dennis Allen's defense. "Still got some room to get better," he says. Perry Knotts / Getty Images
Maybe Cam Lewis has always been wired this way. The Chicago Bears would be grateful.
Growing up in Detroit, the now 29-year-old defensive back said he “just couldn’t stop moving” as a kid. Before a future as a professional football player ever came into view, there was track, soccer and — his favorite — baseball. He was an athlete before he put the pads on at Consortium College Prep (Mich.) as a wide receiver and defensive back. He was, as coaches and teammates still call him today, a Swiss Army Knife.
“You just got to be willing to do things that I wasn’t really comfortable doing at first,” Lewis said of that comparison during an interview at Halas Hall this summer.
With the season opener approaching, Lewis has already lived up to his moniker, channeling his adaptability to play his role on a new-look Bears defense.
“He gets every inch, every ounce out of his body. You’re going to get that out of him,” said Lewis’ college cornerbacks coach, Taiwo Onatolu. “And it’s his love for the game. Some people say it; he never ever talked about it. You just saw it every day.”
In just one summer with the Bears, Lewis has been tested across the secondary. He opened training camp filling in at nickel for Kyler Gordon, who is sidelined indefinitely with a calf injury. Then, when prized free-agent signing Coby Bryant went down with a knee injury in early August, the coaching staff asked Lewis to turn his attention to safety. Lewis spent the back half of camp taking starting safety snaps opposite rookie Dillon Thienemen.
Lewis’ versatility intrigued the Bears during their relatively quiet free-agent shopping in March. He spent his first seven NFL seasons with the Buffalo Bills, starting 14 games and contributing at corner, nickel and safety.
“Every person on the team has a role; no one is more important than the other. But here’s the thing: you got to own your role, and that’s what Cam does really well,” Bears assistant defensive backs coach Matt Giordano said in August. “He understands he can play multiple spots. … He’s a true pro at it and works at his craft every day to maintain a high level of football.”
Lewis didn’t get much time to warm up to his new team before his role changed from plug-and-play depth piece to potential starter. On the unofficial Week 1 depth chart, Lewis was listed as the starting defensive nickelback, though rookie Malik Muhammad could start in Week 1, as he has been the first-team nickel for most of the summer.
Either way, Lewis’ impact will be key for a team missing starters in the secondary.
“I play wherever you need me to play,” Lewis said. “Football is a great team sport, and I love it so much because it’s not individual-based. That’s why I can play safety, I can go play nickel, I can go play dime if you need me to, I can go play special teams.
“It’s not about me; I play for the whole team, the whole city, and just try to go out there and play my best. That’s the only thing I can do.”
For as soft-spoken as Lewis can be, there’s an edge to him that dates to his days at the University at Buffalo. Onatolu, the former Bulls cornerbacks coach, remembers when Lewis arrived on campus as a stocky, 5-foot-9, 170-pound freshman. The coaches thought Lewis would redshirt his first year until they saw him in practice. Even now, Onatolu describes Lewis as the “toughest kid I’ve ever coached or been around.”
“He just was always this quick, explosive, physical player that played bigger than he was,” Onatolu said. “He didn’t say a whole lot. A very, very quiet kid and just kind of handled his business. But he’s really, really passionate about football. And you saw that right away.”
Lewis played in all 12 of Buffalo’s games as a freshman, working his way into a starting cornerback role as a sophomore. He also took snaps at safety, on special teams and at nickel, which in certain packages played more like a weakside linebacker, Onatolu said.
Lewis calls it “cross-training,” the ability to play different positions, and says he’s been doing it his entire career. Former Bulls quarterback Tyree Jackson remembers times in the college offseason when Lewis would run routes for him on the practice field. The two have remained friends since college and, afterward, navigated their adjustments to the NFL as undrafted free-agent signings of the Bills.
“I think anyone that gets to know (Lewis) off the field would just say he’s a great person, but on the field, he definitely has a switch, and he’s a different kind of animal,” Jackson said. “It’s interesting. He’s not always talking loud, but his play is loud.”
With no invitation to the NFL combine, Lewis didn’t have high expectations for the 2019 draft. Instead, he focused on where he could create an opportunity for himself and made an impression on the Bills during their local pro day.
Lewis remembers walking into the locker room for his first day of Bills practice. He introduced himself to his new teammate whose locker stall was next to his. Less than one hour later, that player was cut.
That’s when Lewis realized his versatility wasn’t just a talent. It was a lifeline.
“You always got to compete; every day is an opportunity to continue to prove yourself, to put your best foot forward, to show why you need to be here,” Lewis said. “They always want to bring somebody in to replace you; that’s how I look at it.”
In Buffalo, Lewis worked his way up from the practice squad to become a consistent contributor, playing in all 17 games in each of the last three seasons. When free agency came this spring, Lewis said he knew he and his family would likely be leaving Buffalo, their football home for the past 11 years, which wasn’t particularly easy for his wife, Alexis, and their three young children.
But Chicago presented a new beginning, which Lewis welcomed. He joined a team looking to build on last season’s success, something Lewis knows a thing or two about. His teams in Buffalo never won fewer than 10 games and won the AFC East in five of his seven years. Lewis said success was often player-led, with team dinners and bonding events forming the foundation for the team’s identity. He said he’d like to help build similar camaraderie in Chicago.
On the field, even though Lewis may be familiar with preparing to play multiple spots, that doesn’t mean it comes easy to him. After one late-August practice, Lewis was particularly candid about the learning curve. Practice ended with a long live drill, and Lewis expressed frustration after allowing quarterback Caleb Williams to complete a scramble-drill deep shot to tight end Coleston Loveland for 55 yards.
“I don’t feel like I made enough plays on the ball,” Lewis said afterward. “I do my job to communicate fairly well, but I don’t know. It’s just not up to my standard. It feels a little rocky.
“I’m still learning the defense, how (defensive coordinator Dennis Allen) wants it to be played. …  Coaches may feel like it was a pretty good camp, but to me it doesn’t feel that way. So still got some room to get better, and that’s a good thing.”
The coaching staff used the preseason to make decisions in the secondary. After the final preseason game against Tennessee, Allen said the picture was becoming clearer but wouldn’t elaborate on what that meant for the lineup. The Bears signed veteran Xavier Woods after Bryant’s injury and listed him as the Week 1 starter at safety on the unofficial depth chart.
There are certainly question marks on the Bears defense, and shuffling within the secondary could trickle into early weeks of the season. But come Sunday in Carolina, all that matters is if the team can find the right answers.
“I can tell Ben wants to win. He wants to score points, and (Allen) wants the offense to fear you. That’s how you’re supposed to play defense,” Lewis said. “We still got to grow. It’s still early, going to be a…

full_text:
“You get to the end of training camp, and you're fighting the urge to want to get to this point of the year,” quarterback Caleb Williams said. Andy Lyons / Getty Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — By Sunday, 239 days will have passed since Caleb Williams’ pass intended for DJ Moore was picked off by the Los Angeles Rams’ Kam Curl at Soldier Field, which means 239 days of waiting for this Chicago Bears season to begin.
That’s almost eight months of talking, worrying and dreaming about the Bears.
There is no offseason from a city’s and a fanbase’s obsession, but last season has long been over, a fact that coach Ben Johnson has belabored since his team bowed out of the playoffs on an overtime field goal last January.
It had been some time since the Bears had won a playoff game, as they did last January in a dramatic win over the Green Bay Packers. Fifteen years, to be exact.
In the 2011 season following that previous postseason victory, the Bears started strong but fell apart after an injury to the quarterback. Six more seasons would pass before a return to the playoffs.
That was in 2018, Matt Nagy’s first season as coach. The next year, the Bears finished four games worse and out of the playoffs.
Flash forward to last year and, well, you know the rest.
Sustained success has been about as common at Halas Hall as a 4,000-yard passer, and Johnson is an aware Bear.
“I recognize that last year was a cool season, OK? It was for the players, for the staff, for the city,” Johnson told The Athletic ’s Kevin Fishbain and Dan Wiederer recently . “I recognize that, and I don’t want to downplay that. That was an incredible experience, something that I will never forget.
“At the same time, I also know recent history in Chicago has been, you can have a flash-in-the-pan season, and then the next season it (disappears). You know? We don’t want that. Nobody wants that.”
What Bears fans want is twofold: a competitive present and a future with possibility. It sounds easy but has proven almost impossible. (Kind of like the stadium deal.)
Chicago fell in love with the franchise again last season because the Bears won a lot of games, beat the Packers twice (with some high drama) and showed their fans that their dreams of a high-level coach-quarterback pairing weren’t just a fantasy.
Last season is indeed a memory, but what a memory it was. Building off that is the goal.
“Sure, we want to do big things this year,” Johnson said, “but really what’s most important to us is that we’re laying the foundation the right way.”
Once again, Chicago is fired up for the Bears, and the Bears are fired up about the Bears. It’s also easy to sense an appropriate amount of skepticism in the air. The Bears have unanswered questions.
Last year, the defense couldn’t stop the run and rarely sacked the opposing quarterback, but the defense survived because it relied on a league-leading amount of takeaways. The guys who created them are all somewhere else. The party line at Halas Hall is they’ll have to rely on better coaching to get more production.
There were no massive additions to the roster in the offseason. No trades for Myles Garrett or Maxx Crosby. Bears general manager Ryan Poles had already pledged free-agent money to defensive players in recent years, and the jury is still out on his decisions, to put it nicely. With a limited budget to work with, the Bears seemingly lost as much or more than they gained. They drafted a safety with their first-round pick and added depth on both sides of the ball.
But there are holes in the defense that weren’t patched up. Braxton Jones is starting at left tackle out of necessity. The team’s top free-agent addition, safety Coby Bryant, will start the season on injured reserve. Kyler Gordon, expected to be one of the team’s reliable cornerbacks, is rehabbing a mysterious leg injury away from the team.
It’s as if there’s a flashing sign outside of Halas Hall that says “Regression.” I think 10-7 is a reasonable expectation, if not a little optimistic, considering the team’s schedule. Johnson won’t have to look hard for bulletin-board material if the Bears lose some games early.
“We’re the No. 1 regression candidate,” Johnson said as training camp opened, “so I think we got plenty of motivation ourselves.”
Still, the mood around the Bears is high almost entirely because of the talent and potential of the Williams-and-Johnson pairing. For once, the Bears seemed to have gotten the coach and quarterback right.
There are heightened expectations for a variety of complementary players (will Colston Loveland have a breakout season?), and there will be increased scrutiny for others as well (can Dayo Odeyingbo and Montez Sweat get loose?).
The playoffs are a realistic expectation for the Bears, and all it will take to go from “making it” to “Super Bowl or bust” is a couple of victories. Maybe just a win this Sunday in the season opener in Carolina, where the Bears are favored by a field goal.
What we know is the Bears can’t control the noise, and Chicago is a loud place when the football season begins.
“Expectations,” Williams said this week, “I think they start from internal for us.”
Behind closed doors, Johnson is painfully honest with his players about their mistakes in the present, but he’s also a motivator, which involves making his guys believe anything is possible.
Cornerback Jaylon Johnson said he recently had a one-on-one talk with his coach. The message was simple: We need you to step up and help us get to the Super Bowl.
“When he said that, it put some things in perspective for me, and I have — we have — the opportunity to do something special,” he said.
Perhaps this is a bad trait for a sportswriter, but I’m not that interested in what the Bears can be come January or Williams’ place in the QB hierarchy. It just doesn’t feel important right now. We have had so much free time to wonder about what the Bears can be. The beauty of the season starting Sunday is that we have something tangible to judge them on.
“You get to the end of training camp, and you’re fighting the urge to want to get to this point of the year,” Williams said. “You’re excited to be here, and it all matters now. Everything we did, everything we’re going to do, on that field out here, is going to matter on game day.”
We don’t know where the Bears will finish, but we know they’re 0-0 now. The future is upon them.

full_text:
Cashius Howell celebrates a fumble recovery during the Bengals' preseason win over the Lions. Sam Greene / Imagn Images
CINCINNATI — Joe Burrow isn’t lying. He’s also not leaving any room for speculation.
Not only did he make it clear this week that he has no plans to leave Cincinnati and will be with the Bengals “for the long haul,” but he also added another telling comment, peeling back how he feels about his team’s chances in 2026.
“I would say I’m more excited this year than I’ve been in a long time,” he said Wednesday. “I’ve always been excited to play, but this year I’m excited to watch, too. I’m just really excited to see our guys go make it happen.”
The excitement is undeniable in a Bengals locker room overflowing with good vibes and notably lacking traditional distractions and landmines. This goes beyond the typical optimism of this time of year and the confidence emanating from every corner of the roster tells as much of a story as the trade for Dexter Lawrence.
Burrow’s belief comes from what he witnessed coming to life on the other side of the ball. He might finally have a defense to support him for the first time in three years.
No need to be a hero every drive. No need to take unnecessary chances because a shootout is inevitable. No need to ditch patience with the run game to keep defenses honest.
One of the most interesting talking points entering the season for the Bengals revolves around the star quarterback not needing to put on the Superman suit every week. That’s a freeing concept for him in Year 7 and, yeah, it might just be fun for him to watch again.
Let’s take a closer look at what else I’ve been seeing and hearing about this team in the weeks leading up to Sunday’s opener.
Perhaps the least talked-about impactful addition to the Bengals’ pass rush is second-round pick Cashius Howell. Well, least talked about outside the facility. Internally, people can’t stop talking about how good Howell looked during camp.
“Hitting on Cashius,” defensive coordinator Al Golden began, “I can’t underscore how important that is because he’s come through for us in terms of his intellect, his work ethic, his ability to process, and his learning curve.”
Think about that for a minute. Golden’s already declaring Howell a “hit.” The 2025 SEC Defensive Player of the Year hasn’t even played a game yet.
He ran circles around the Bengals’ backup tackles and produced similarly when elevated to line up against the first team. He was a major factor in finishing off the Bears in the joint practice.
There were moments when veterans were able to stand him up and slow him down; tight end Drew Sample notably enjoyed one such moment, but the excitement grew when Howell started learning from his mistakes and seeing the vision.
He didn’t miss a day, a practice or a meeting since being selected 41st.
“He’s gotten exponentially better with every rep,” head coach Zac Taylor said, pointing out that he’s spent extra time working with position coaches. “I feel really good about where he’s at right now. He’s done everything he can to be used at the maximum volume.”
The Bengals didn’t need to see Howell beyond the first preseason game, instead opting to unleash him fully against Tampa Bay. He’ll still feature in subpackages among the deep edge group, but he’ll be present in high-leverage moments.
Cincinnati’s rookie record for sacks was set by Carlos Dunlap in 2010 with 9.5. Carl Lawson notched 8.5 as a rookie in 2017. Howell would probably need an injury in front of him to expand his role enough to match those two, but the Bengals anticipate him producing in the vicinity of those numbers. I’d place a personal over/under on 5.5 sacks and 34 pressures.
The clock ticks close to midnight on the Bengals’ big four contract extension candidates. Cincinnati traditionally opts not to negotiate extensions during the season and has stuck by that with rare exceptions.
Will DJ Turner, Dax Hill, Chase Brown or Myles Murphy sneak on the wire? Highly unlikely.
Despite opportunities to nail down a long-term deal before the price potentially goes up after this season, these four all look prepared to determine the biggest contract of their life on the field.
Turner was thought to be the most likely (and most expensive) in a skyrocketing cornerback market that saw the latest agreement with New England’s Christian Gonzalez on Tuesday for four years, $135 million and $102 million in guarantees.
The two sides aren’t near a deal, and Turner reiterated in recent days his comfort playing out the final year of his rookie contract. He’s been a full participant since the offseason program, was named a captain and sounds determined to prove he’s worth every penny available at the top of the market after this year.
The Lawrence deal changed the Bengals’ math this offseason, and de facto general manager Duke Tobin spoke before training camp about the future outlays and challenges in completing those deals.
The negotiations have stayed out of sight, out of mind, with everyone happily participating in camp and one of the players even mentioned they forgot that it was even going on while grinding through camp.
“I’m proud of those guys,” Taylor said. “I haven’t felt it for one second from any of them. They have all come to work every single day. They have had a great mindset, a great attitude.”
Plenty can change in one season and the Bengals sound content to see where the market lands for these four. And the four sound content to bet on themselves, hoping the price goes up just as it did for Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins two years ago. The Bengals have a franchise tag at their disposal to contain one, but otherwise could well be forced to see all three hit the open market if they can’t agree to a deal.
Bengals’ assistant Jordan Salkin stood up in a team meeting Wednesday, pointing out how much the team’s success will lead to individual milestones. Those four are undeniably banking on it.
How much will the Bengals utilize the under-center portion of the playbook they spent so much time practicing in recent months? That’s a concept offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher posed from the moment he first spoke to the team in the spring, and he’s keeping the results understandably close to the vest.
“The No. 1 thing we want to be is a team and offense that can be whoever we need to be to win the game,” Pitcher said. “That’s the first slide I put up in front of the group this spring. All our efforts with regard to what we spent our time on schematically were aimed towards that, so we have confidence in a bigger universe that we can pull from. I don’t know game in and game out what that is going to look like. If I did, I wouldn’t tell you.”
Pitcher and company have an idea, of course. The under-center offense honed itself after a rocky start to training camp and never went away. There are internal benchmarks they would like to hit in utilizing under-center and under-center play action, but those could vary widely from game to game.
Those benchmarks project to at least double the amount the Bengals have used over the last four seasons, if believing the chatter over time about leaning back into the 2021 philosophy for using that weapon to create explosives.
If teams opt to play light boxes and lean into cloud coverage, which the Bengals have seen at a rate far higher than anybody in the NFL over the last two years, they feel much more prepared to push that button as a solution.
We do know this. They feel more freedom putting the game plan together this week, knowing the reps banked on an expanded menu.
“I feel like we have arrived at a point here in Week 1 where we have a good sense of the things we are going to be able to execute at a high level,” Pitcher said. “And the time we’ve invested has been time well spent.”
There’s a different tone you hear about certain players this time of year. Almost everyone has nice things said about them. That’s the nature of optimism season.

title: Deshaun Watson, with Todd Monken's support, gets another shot to prove himself Monken is beginning his tenure as the Browns' head coach by placing his faith in Watson. But now comes the hard part. Zac Jackson 12

If you’re caught up on everything without having incurred motion sickness, perhaps you’re just numb to it all by no
full_text:
Deshaun Watson will start for the first time since October 2024 when the Browns face the Jaguars in Week 1. Jason Miller / Getty Images
As the 2026 season kicks off and the Cleveland Browns’ perpetual quarterback carousel spins, next up in the big chair — the one with no seat belt — are a new head coach who’s an older guy and a quarterback who’s not new but hopes for a fresh start.
If you’re caught up on everything without having incurred motion sickness, perhaps you’re just numb to it all by now. Or maybe you’re like coach Todd Monken and are truly optimistic this can work, and that the Browns going back to Deshaun Watson in the final year of his albatross contract can lead to positive results.
Monken, 60, is a head coach for the first time since he was at Southern Miss more than a decade ago and the first time in the NFL. Watson, 31 next week, hasn’t played a regular-season down in about 23 months and — outside of maybe three games — hasn’t played well since he arrived in Cleveland in 2022 with $230 million in guarantees and an 11-game suspension for multiple violations of the NFL’s personal conduct policy.
The organization is still playing catch-up after it traded three first-round picks to the Houston Texans for the right to give Watson that contract. The Browns enter 2026 as one of the league’s youngest teams, and in June they traded two-time Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett to the Los Angeles Rams for defensive end Jared Verse and three draft picks, most notably a 2027 first-rounder.
Watson has played 19 games in four years with the Browns. He had 20 300-yard passing games in his four seasons as the Texans’ starter, but none with Cleveland. In 2024, when he last played in a meaningful game, Watson didn’t reach 200 passing yards during his seven starts before he suffered a torn right Achilles tendon. He tore the same tendon again a little more than two months later and missed the 2025 season.
The Browns said they were moving on. But with no answer at the game’s most important position coming out of a season that ended with the firing of two-time Coach of the Year Kevin Stefanski , their intended path forward instead led them back to Watson, who says he’s healthy and motivated to “thrive” and deliver “the best product” the Browns thought they were getting 4 1/2 years ago.
“I’m super excited, just super happy,” Watson said Wednesday. “I’m super blessed for the opportunity that this organization gave me, and I just want to be able to capitalize on it. So right now I’m just present in this moment, getting ready for practice and just letting the days come to me.
“I don’t want to rush it, and I don’t want to try to drag it on. I just kind of, again, enjoy each moment because I know how fast it can be taken away. So I just continue to just focus on my present.”
After being hired in late January , Monken conducted a quarterback competition that ran from the first day of voluntary offseason workouts in early April until the second preseason game in late August. Monken always believed Watson would win based on his experience and Monken’s belief that Watson can still create on the move.
With the Browns opening the season with two straight road games and six of their first nine on the road, Monken went with Watson and his 72 career starts over Shedeur Sanders and his seven .
But two days before Monken announced his decision, Watson played with backups in the third quarter of the Browns’ preseason game versus the Buffalo Bills. Home fans booed Watson at least four times. After the game, he responded angrily and told reporters he didn’t know if he could handle the negativity, saying he might have to approach the season as if there are 17 road games.
Now, Watson said Wednesday, he’s “not worried about that.”
Monken addressed the comments and the situation with Watson first, then publicly. The new coach stands behind his quarterback and believes — even if nobody outside the building does — that Watson has moved forward and is ready to resume a once-promising career for a franchise that bet big on him and, so far, has seen no positive returns.
“We focus on what we can do now,” Watson said. “So, it’s not about what we’re worried about in the future or in the past. We’re not worried about 2024. We’re not worried about last year, me not playing. We’re not worried about the preseason. Right now, we’ve got to focus on Jacksonville.”
On Sunday, Watson returns to the field with a remade Browns offense against a Jaguars team that won 13 games last season and has three first-round picks on its defensive line. Monken, who’s clearly unburdened by the past, believes Watson can eventually be the same. And with a talented young group of offensive skill players and a new staff calling the shots, Monken thinks the Browns will show up ready to play.
The Browns’ starters played only two preseason series as a full unit, then had one joint practice session with the Bills. Based on glimpses of that and what Monken has said, we can expect an offense that looks to get Watson out of the pocket — and maybe even use him as a runner at times — in hopes of finding the player who, in four seasons with the Texans, was a 68 percent passer who averaged 8.3 yards per attempt.
In Cleveland, Watson has completed just 61 percent of his passes at 6.0 yards per attempt with 19 touchdowns and 12 interceptions over parts of three seasons.
“We’re certainly going to try to build it as best we can around the things we’ve seen in the months we’ve been around Deshaun (and) what we think gives us all, offensively, a chance to operate at a really high level,” Monken said. “So, I’m excited for him. I’ve said that all along for all the work he’s put in.
“He has really embraced what we do offensively. I think for him it’s been a breath of fresh air, new life, new opportunity. Now, we’ve all got to take advantage of it — same with myself.”
Monken, who’s been overseeing high-speed practices and losing his voice since the spring, acknowledged there’s a new energy inside the team facility this week now that the season is here. He’s anxious for Watson, all three of his first-time coordinators, gifted rookie wide receivers KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston and all involved to hit the field.
“It should feel like it’s different (this week),” Monken said. “It’s everything we work for. That’s why we get paid what we get paid, right? It should feel different to put our best foot forward (in practice) today, and then tomorrow … and then go play our best football on Sunday.”
He knows, too, the stakes — and the perception — of his decision to go with Watson. Monken said he’s seen and experienced enough in his four decades in coaching to believe he’s “well prepared for the ups and downs that are coming.” Twenty seasons after he got his first NFL job as the Jaguars’ wide receivers coach, he’s the next head coach of the Browns, a team many believe is playing for next year.
Monken says he’ll have his team ready and is putting his trust in Watson, who knows he’s getting an opportunity he wasn’t promised — and might not get again.
“I’ve got to focus on now,” Watson said. “If I try to look ahead and I get distracted or am not focusing on what I need to do now, then who knows what the future might hold. … And like coach Monken said, he’s 60. He feels like this is his shot. So, me being on my last year of my deal and being in Year 10, I feel like this is my opportunity to be able to go and showcase that I can still play in this league.
“I want to continue to play in this league. So this is my opportunity to do that.”

full_text:
Can Christian Parker get the Dallas defense turned around? The Cowboys think he's the right guy. Kirby Lee / Imagn Images
FRISCO, Texas — The Dallas Cowboys offense is supposed to be excellent this season. Their defense, however, has many questions to answer.
So, it was no surprise when KaVontae Turpin caught a deep ball from Dak Prescott while facing Dallas’ starting defense on the first day of training camp. There was an important detail, though. The play came after it appeared that Prescott was pressured by the defensive front.
There’s no hitting the quarterback in practice, so defenders run by if they win on a rush.
Christian Parker knew what happened.
“That’s a lot of f–––ing cardio for a sack,” the team’s new defensive coordinator yelled in the direction of Turpin and other Cowboys receivers running back to the huddle. Parker and Turpin then slapped hands.
Parker wanted to make sure the offense knew the play was a notable win for the defense. The 34-year-old carries a no-nonsense, locked-in appearance during practice, but he also has a reputation for being one of the team’s biggest trash-talkers.
“I would say the s––– talking from Christian Parker is a little different than what we had last year,” Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said in June. “The guys feed off of it in a good way, and you (reporters) are beginning to figure out his personality, in a good way. It’s been fun to watch him stir up CeeDee (Lamb), George (Pickens), Dak and those guys. I think we’re in a really good spot.”
Parker has been tasked with turning arguably the worst defense in franchise history into one that is at least respectable. Witnessing what they have been trying to accomplish since rookie minicamp, it’s realistic to expect a much improved product come Sunday night in New Jersey.
The roster has been upgraded. Defensive tackle Kenny Clark, cornerback DaRon Bland and safety Malik Hooker are the only starters remaining from last year’s season opener. The other eight aren’t even on the roster.
The Cowboys’ other notable defensive roster moves included drafting outside linebacker Malachi Lawrence in the first round, signing veteran outside linebacker Von Miller, signing veteran defensive tackles Otito Ogbonnia and Jonathan Bullard, drafting inside linebacker Jaishawn Barham and signing veteran safety P.J. Locke.
Parker has been working to utilize that personnel in a transition from a 4-3 to 3-4 base defense that is expected to cause problems by keeping opposing quarterbacks uncomfortable.
“One of his really premium goals is to mix it up and be unpredictable,” Cowboys owner Jerry Jones said on 105.3 The Fan before their preseason opener in Seattle. “That really takes a lot of communication. That takes a lot of coordination. Bottom line is, I think he’s got all the ingredients. Not only is he a motivator, communicator, but he’s got the ingredients to be a very strategic outstanding coach.”
Parker’s hands-on coaching style has been witnessed throughout practices going back to rookie minicamp. Many have talked about his ability to relate to players with examples going beyond what is seen on the field.
“I think it’s important when you’re communicating in the heat of the moment, the relationships matter,” Schottenheimer said. “There are a lot of times where you are making a correction, and if you don’t have the relationship, if you don’t have the buy-in from the players at times, players, coaches as well, can tune you out.
“I don’t think there’s any chance of that happening, because he’s built up a rapport with these guys.”
Schottenheimer has often talked about the individual time Parker has been spending in his office with players going over film. There were far too many communication issues last season. The extra time should help eliminate those carrying over into this season.
“If you don’t have that, I think it hurts your ability to critique, coach, coach hard and call out,” Schottenheimer said. “They need to know you love them and care about them. So, if you don’t spend the time doing that, you’re missing an opportunity.
“I think (his youth) does help. I didn’t go to three nights straight of Jay-Z (concerts) in New York City. He did. Four or five of our players were there. … I do think that the age does help. They are into the same things. He’s got some really expensive shoes. He’s got some really expensive watches. And so do our players. … That’s real. That’s real that you can relate to your guys like that.”
While Parker has been seen working with many, no one appears to be getting more individual time than rookie Caleb Downs . The first-round pick is expected to be one of the biggest factors in Dallas’ defensive turnaround. He will be deployed in a variety of ways as a do-everything defensive back who can help in all areas. One play he could be stepping up to stop the run or blitz the quarterback and the next he could be dropping into coverage against a wide receiver, running back or tight end.
Defensive back is Parker’s speciality. He was a cornerbacks coach when he got his start in college at Virginia State in 2013. After moving up the college ranks, his first NFL job was a defensive quality control coach with the Green Bay Packers before becoming defensive backs coach for the Denver Broncos in 2021. The previous two seasons were spent as the defensive backs coach and defensive passing game coordinator with the Philadelphia Eagles.
The defensive backfield should be much improved with Parker’s coaching and the personnel upgrades. But will they have enough pass rush in his first year as a defensive coordinator? That’s where his coaching will see the biggest test. Can he find consistent ways to scheme up things to make opposing quarterbacks hold the ball a little longer?
It certainly sounds like he has no problem putting in the extra hours to figure it out. His preparation and attention to detail has been a common theme when others have talked about Parker.
“I don’t even want to talk about that,” Parker said when asked about how little sleep he gets. “It’s not something I’m necessarily proud of. But the job has to get done and you kind of go down a rabbit hole sometimes and you look up at the clock and you missed that time. You try to get as much preparation as you can during the week and then catch up at the end.”
There has been so much positive momentum since Parker was hired in January that outside speculation has already shifted to him having too much immediate success and other teams looking to him as a future head-coaching candidate.
The Cowboys have lost only one coordinator to a head-coaching job in the last 30 years and that was Dan Quinn two years ago to Washington. Before that, you have to go all the way back to Butch Davis becoming the Miami Hurricanes head coach in 1995 and Norv Turner becoming Washington’s head coach in 1994.
Parker getting head-coaching interest would be a good problem for the Cowboys, knowing it would be coming because of a very successful defense.
“What (our) talent needs is what he’s bringing to the table,” Jones said Tuesday on The Fan. “The right kind of communication, the right kind of tone-setting with expectation. He’s got the team believing in what he’s trying to do, it’s something that they can execute on. He’s got a great bunch, a can-do bunch.”
The first step is looking like an improved bunch Sunday night against the New York Giants. Schottenheimer and Jones are confident that will happen.
“There’s a difference when you can say, ‘I helped build it. I helped put it together,” Jones said of Parker. “Right before our eyes, I was a part of building that defense that ultimately, if you will, became a Super Bowl defense.’”
The offense is talented enough for the Cowboys to get to the playoffs. But for them to put together a deep playoff run for the first time in 30 years, Parker and his group will likely be the difference. The Cowboys are confident that their first-time defensive coordinator has the ability to make it…

ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — As Bo Nix stepped onto a podium following a Broncos training camp on Aug. 1, he looked across the field toward the team’s recently abandoned, former practice facility, a building soon to be demolished. The stark
full_text:
Bo Nix looks to take the Broncos to the playoffs for the third time in his third NFL season. C. Morgan Engel / Getty Images
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — As Bo Nix stepped onto a podium following a Broncos training camp on Aug. 1, he looked across the field toward the team’s recently abandoned, former practice facility, a building soon to be demolished. Behind him sat the glistening, new $175 million facility he and 400 other members of the organization had begun settling into just days earlier.
The stark change of venue mirrored the “drastically” different mindset Nix said he was bringing into his third season as Denver’s starting quarterback — one he laid out in simple terms.
“Year 1, I’m trying to just not mess up for the team,” Nix said. “I feel like Year 3, I’m trying to make plays for the team. It’s just quite the different feeling. It’s just a confidence-level thing.”
His confidence is built on his results as an NFL starting quarterback, a job Nix won during his first training camp after Denver selected him with the 12th pick in the 2024 draft. He has led the Broncos to the playoffs twice, with the first appearance ending the franchise’s eight-year stretch without a postseason berth. He helped the Broncos wrest the AFC West away from the Kansas City Chiefs for the first time in a decade last season. He outdueled the Buffalo Bills’ Josh Allen to win an overtime playoff game.
Nix has accounted for more touchdowns than any player in his draft class, and no quarterback has won more games through his first two seasons than the 24 victories he helped produce for the Broncos in 2024 and 2025.
Yet, Nix can be like a fluffy cumulus cloud passing through the sky on a summer day. One member of the football-consuming public can stare up and see a certain kind of quarterback. Another could look at the cloud and see a different passer entirely. Nix does not make the top 10 in preseason quarterback polls. Critics point to a history of ankle injuries, often leaving out that Nix has started 63 of a possible 64 games over the past four seasons, dating back to his time at Oregon.
The sports talk show circuit has been so jammed with narratives about Nix this offseason that his head coach, veteran Sean Payton, felt compelled to jump on social media to dispel a take he found particularly egregious .
“It’s the one cool thing about our sport,” Payton said. “You could argue, at any position, a top 10, and (in) all of those discussions, generally, time will give you those answers. We love what we’re seeing (from Nix). Again, they’re measured by wins, and they’re measured by certain things. Ultimately, that’s how history will be written about any of them, the quarterbacks specifically.”
Nix is carrying it all onto the precipice of the biggest season of his football life, which begins with the Broncos’ Week 1 opener at Kansas City on Monday night. He will be eligible for a massive contract extension as soon as next offseason. In a ballooning quarterback market that has 13 players at the position currently making more than $50 million annually, including two over $60 million, it’s not outlandish to envision a new long-term deal for Nix that makes him the franchise’s first $300 million man if he puts together the kind of season he and the Broncos believe he is capable of producing. It’s a decision that will impact how Denver goes about building a Super Bowl contender in the years to come.
The quarterback is handling that pressure in much the same way he’s handled it while leading an NFL-high 10 game-winning drives across the past two seasons: by naming it.
“Competitively, the way we are as players, you better treat every year as a year you have to prove it,” Nix said. “You have to go out there and show the team that you’re worth what they’re putting in for you and what they’re building around you. You can’t ever let up and think that, ‘I’ve made it. I’ve gotten to where I need to be.’ Quite honestly, I’ll never feel that way.
“There’s always the next season. There’s always the next championship to go after. I think every year for every player is going to feel like a contract year, because it should.”
When Davis Webb took over as the Broncos’ offensive coordinator in February, he quickly built a project designed to analyze Nix’s first two seasons as Denver’s starting quarterback. Every decision. Every throw. The goal was to tweak the scheme to highlight Nix’s strengths and find areas where the quarterback and the offense could still grow. The process helped move the Broncos toward their offseason acquisition of Jaylen Waddle, a dynamic target who has already demonstrated an ability to bend the defense’s geometry in a favorable way for his quarterback.
Nix, as he rehabbed from the ankle injury that forced him to miss January’s AFC championship game, was breaking down his own game in a similar way.
“The one thing you’re seeing from him is he’s trusting his throws — a lot,” tight end Adam Trautman said as he found refuge in a quiet, air-conditioned corner of the team’s indoor field after a sweltering camp practice last month. “With his timing, there are some tight windows he’s throwing into now that maybe before, in years past, it was, ‘Eh, maybe I’m not going to take a shot there. I’m going to check it down.’ He’s trusting himself, and it’s cool to see because you can always get the ball. It doesn’t matter what you’re feeling in coverage; he’ll rip it in there.
“He’s coming in here now, and it’s not like, ‘Oh, I’m afraid to mess up.’ It’s ‘Now I’m the guy. I need to get better, too. I need to trust the things that I’ve worked on in the offseason.’ This is the best training camp he’s had, for sure.”
Nix illustrated his aggressiveness in training camp with whom he was willing to attack: namely, All-Pro corner Pat Surtain II. As a rookie and a quarterback who built a reputation on being a mistake-averse passer, Nix rarely looked Surtain’s way, let alone threw the ball near him. Even in his second training camp, you likely could have counted on one hand the number of times Nix attacked the superstar defensive back.
That changed in August as Nix challenged the best player on the team almost daily. Nix reached a notable milestone when he hit Waddle on a deep touchdown pass after he got a step on Surtain, but the quarterback learned just as much from coming up on the wrong end of that battle.
“My first two years, if (Surtain) was over there, I pretty much worked to the other side of the field, but I don’t think that does him (any) diligence,” Nix said. “Now that I feel a little bit more confident and comfortable, I don’t mind throwing it his way and getting an incompletion on the stat sheet just to help him out every once in a while.
“He does a really good job, and every once in a while, when we get to complete one on him, it kind of feels good for the morale of the offense. It shows us that we’re also really good and we can attack the best player in football on defense.”
The trust isn’t only evident in what Nix believes his arm can do. It also shows up in how he is processing what he sees on the other side of the line of scrimmage. Nix has always been a chore to “sack” during camp practices due to his mobility and elusiveness, All-Pro defensive end Zach Allen said recently. But the task is more difficult in this camp with Nix finding new areas of the field to exploit.
“Definitely now, the way he reads defenses, it’s second to none,” Allen said. “It really is impressive how elite he is. The big thing everyone talks about is how few sacks he takes. It really is a struggle. The offensive line he has is really good, but he gets the ball out quick. Seeing him be comfortable in his third year is awesome.”
Payton visibly cringed early in training camp when he was asked about the notion of a “Year 3 leap” for Nix. He pointed to the quarterback’s resumé of winning games, including a franchise-record-tying 14 victories in 2025. Then, the coach reframed the question.

full_text:
Kyler Murray and Jonathan Gannon are familiar with each other from their days with the Cardinals. Michael Chow / Imagn Images
GREEN BAY, Wis. — Jonathan Gannon cautioned reporters before he began answering questions at the podium on Tuesday.
“I’m not in the mode of this right now, so excuse me if I don’t come off great,” he said.
Tuesday is the primary game-planning day for coaches whose teams play on Sunday, and Gannon was in the middle of prepping for his first regular-season game as Green Bay Packers defensive coordinator.
“Once we get back into the flow, I’ll be better,” he said.
Most coaches saunter off the podium after answering questions. Gannon zipped off the lectern when he was done. He had work to do, though that might not be as complicated as in other weeks since Gannon is intimately familiar with the Minnesota Vikings quarterback he’ll face in Week 1.
“Kyler Murray, really good player,” said Gannon, who was Murray’s head coach in Arizona the last three seasons. “He’s in a really good offense with some elite players. Obviously, I’ve got nothing but love and respect for ‘K1.’ He’s competitive, he’s smart, can make all the throws and beat you with his legs, so big-time challenge.”
Gannon knows everything about Murray. What he’s good at and what he isn’t. Perhaps more so the latter after the Cardinals benched their former franchise quarterback last season in favor of Jacoby Brissett. Gannon and Murray played a role in the Cardinals going 15-36 over the last three seasons, which is why both had to find new jobs during the offseason. Now they’ll meet at U.S. Bank Stadium after weeks of game planning against each other instead of with each other, but who has the advantage?
“I’d say (Gannon) probably knows exactly what (Murray) likes and doesn’t like,” Packers head coach Matt LaFleur said. “But again, it’s a different scheme, a different system. There’s 10 other guys out there, and I think that’s a pretty good supporting cast he’s got around him. There’s a lot of playmakers out there. I think their O-line is one of the better O-lines in the league, so they’ve got a lot of talent around him.”
One would assume Gannon has a slight advantage over Murray because a quarterback’s skill set, tendencies and ticks are what they are, even if his supporting cast and play caller are different. On the flip side, Gannon’s core principles on defense may remain, but the personnel around him probably dictate how he goes about his business more than the pieces around Murray affect what he does.
Don’t expect anyone in the Packers locker room to say that, though, even as Gannon shares his unique insight on Murray with his new team.
“Yeah, he has, but I’m not going to display what he’s told us,” safety Xavier McKinney said. “He has major respect for Kyler and what he’s been able to do in this league. Obviously he’s a playmaker. You know that. He can extend plays with his feet, and we also know he can make the throws down the field, as well, so he’s been a good quarterback in this league, and we respect him.”
Packers standout right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele told The Athletic on Wednesday that he “definitely” expects to play on Sunday.
LaFleur hadn’t answered questions about Bako-Bewele’s availability distinctly this week, and offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich said Tuesday that the team didn’t know who would start on the offensive line in Minnesota, in part because of Bako-Bewele’s health.
Green Bay’s best offensive lineman partially tore his patellar tendon Dec. 14, 2025, the same game in which edge rusher Micah Parsons tore his ACL in Denver. Bako-Bewele, who missed the final four games of the regular season and playoffs, underwent offseason surgery and eased into action during training camp. He didn’t look quite like his normal dominant self, and a recent comment to reporters about his health and how he wasn’t exactly ready yet but would be by Week 1 cast doubt on social media.
Bako-Bewele thought those reactions were over the top and, though he was limited in Wednesday’s practice, he plans to play the full game in Week 1.
“I feel good about Sunday. I feel like I’m definitely gonna be out there,” he said. “I’m not gonna sit here and lie and say it’s been perfect (during camp). There’s been some ups and downs, but I think with where we’re at right now, yeah, I think I’m about as ready as I can feel to play a game … not gonna find out (until) we go out and play, but I feel good about where I’m at.
“When I’m out there, I do expect to perform at an elite level.”
Stenavich said Tuesday that the Packers will play running back by committee “for a little while.” Is that a commentary on how long they expect Josh Jacobs to be out? Perhaps, but it might be more telling that the Packers don’t sound married to having MarShawn Lloyd shoulder the workload of a feature back despite his standing as the de facto No. 1 running back with Jacobs on the commissioner’s exempt list .
Lloyd has played in one game over his first two seasons because of a litany of injuries. Though he said he’s ready for any workload after not missing a single training camp practice, taking hits throughout a game is different than absorbing thuds on Ray Nitschke Field.
“I thought he did a nice job this entire offseason kind of proving to us and himself that he could be out there (regularly), so hopefully we just keep improving and as the season rolls through, we’ll be seeing the best version of him,” Stenavich said of Lloyd. “I’m not going to say like X amount of touches or anything like that, but we definitely want to get him the ball. He does have explosive and playmaking ability.”
If the Packers do play the running back position by committee, that means more touches for Chris Brooks. Primarily a situational third-down back who’s adept at pass protection, Brooks has 63 carries for 289 yards and a touchdown in two years with the Packers, with 24 catches for 160 yards.
“I think he’s done a nice job,” LaFleur said. “I think you saw it last year. He got a lot of opps versus (the Vikings) in that Week 18 game, and I know he was out there, but all their starters were out there. So yeah, I’ve got a lot of confidence in Chris.”
It’s unclear whether newly acquired running back Kaleb Johnson has learned enough to be active on Sunday, while practice squad running back Pierre Strong Jr. missed practice Wednesday with an undisclosed injury.
More clarity on Jacobs’ legal situation may come Thursday morning, when his attorneys are scheduled to appear for his first court hearing at the Brown County Courthouse in Green Bay.
Defensive tackle Warren Brinson (calf) and linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper (Achilles) were the only two members of the 53-man roster not practicing on Wednesday.
The limited participants included Bako-Bewele (knee), left guard Aaron Banks (knee), defensive tackle Javon Hargrave (knee), left tackle Jordan Morgan (knee), edge Barryn Sorrell (foot) and defensive tackle Devonte Wyatt (ankle).

If nothing else, Chris Ballard is a survivor.
