full_text:
Chris Ballard has a 70-78-1 record in nine seasons as the Colts general manager. Robert Goddin / Imagn Images
If nothing else, Chris Ballard is a survivor. Over the past decade, the coaches, players and even owners have changed within the Indianapolis Colts’ franchise, yet the general manager has remained the same. Ballard is entering his 10th season at the helm of the Colts, but his job security isn’t buttressed by his resume. In fact, as you’ll see in our table below, Ballard’s lack of success puts him in a league of his own in terms of the NFL’s longest-tenured GMs.
So why does he keep getting more chances?
With the Colts days away from kicking off their 2026 season, The Athletic took a look back at the nine lives of Chris Ballard, examining each of his nine seasons running the show in Indy to see how he cultivated a 10th. Hint : Sometimes, it’s just good to be liked.
What happened : Andrew Luck missed the entire season due to a shoulder injury. Without their franchise QB, the Colts traded wide receiver Phillip Dorsett to the New England Patriots in exchange for quarterback Jacoby Brissett. Brissett, a 2016 third-round pick, went 4-11 as the starter and threw 13 TDs against seven interceptions. He was also sacked a league-high 52 times. Indianapolis lost six of its last seven games to finish with its worst record since 2011, which was the year before the team drafted Luck.
Why Ballard returned : Ballard was only in his first year at the helm, replacing Ryan Grigson, who went 49-31 in five seasons — Ballard still has yet to surpass Grigson's three playoff wins and two division titles.
Ballard's job security was never in doubt given the unique circumstances he walked into with Luck already being sidelined. The Colts expressed confidence that Luck would make a full recovery, but that didn't stop them from making a significant organizational change by firing coach Chuck Pagano and replacing him with Frank Reich, who was the Philadelphia Eagles' offensive coordinator and had previously worked with Peyton Manning as the Colts' quarterbacks coach.
What happened : Luck returned from his shoulder injury, and the 2012 No. 1 pick quickly flipped the franchise's fortunes. He threw 39 touchdowns against 15 picks en route to being named the NFL’s Comeback Player of the Year while leading the Colts to the playoffs for the first time since the 2014 season. Indianapolis took down the Houston Texans in the wild-card round before falling to the Kansas City Chiefs in the divisional round. The win against the Texans remains Ballard's lone playoff victory.
Why Ballard returned : He wasn’t going anywhere after the Colts’ resurgent campaign. Luck once again looked like the franchise cornerstone they drafted him to be, and his performance throughout the regular season and postseason sparked Indy's hopes of rekindling the Manning glory days and becoming an annual championship contender. No one could’ve predicted what would come next.
What happened : Luck shocked the NFL world by retiring just before the start of the season, which understandably changed the team’s trajectory. Indianapolis subsequently turned to Brissett, who steered the Colts to an impressive 5-2 start, highlighted by a road win over Patrick Mahomes' Chiefs. However, Brissett's play tapered off after he was hobbled by a knee injury. Indy lost five of its final six games as it became abundantly clear that the team needed to upgrade at quarterback.
Why Ballard returned : Ballard was thrown one of the craziest curveballs in league history and arguably all of sports. Luck, the player who had successfully filled the giant shoes left by Manning, walked away from football at just 29 years old. The four-time Pro Bowler cited a cycle of injury, pain and rehab for his abrupt retirement, which gave the Colts no time to find a long-term replacement. All things considered, Indianapolis fared pretty well in the first year of Luck's absence, and the franchise felt good about the rest of the roster Ballard had put together.
What happened : Indy signed Philip Rivers (the first time!) to a one-year deal, and the eight-time Pro Bowler delivered for Ballard and the Colts. Rivers threw 24 touchdowns against 11 interceptions to lead the Colts to the playoffs alongside breakout star Jonathan Taylor. The rookie running back totaled 253 rushing yards in a regular-season finale win over the Jacksonville Jaguars to punch Indy's ticket to the postseason. The Colts narrowly lost to the Buffalo Bills in the wild-card round, falling just short of a fourth-quarter rally.
Why Ballard returned : The Colts' playoff berth completed a remarkable turnaround in the wake of Luck's retirement, and late team owner Jim Irsay made sure to commend Ballard for his team-building, highlighted by the acquisition of Rivers. Even after Rivers retired (the first time!), Irsay said the Colts were "capable of competing for the Super Bowl very soon," so long as Ballard found a suitable replacement. About that ...
(It's also worth noting that just ahead of the 2021 season, Irsay furnished Ballard and Reich with contract extensions that carried them through the 2026 season.)
What happened : After Rivers retired, the Colts traded a 2021 third-round pick and what ended up being a 2022 first-round pick to the Philadelphia Eagles in exchange for Carson Wentz. Wentz, the 2016 No. 2 pick, threw 27 touchdowns against seven picks. His performance was aided by Taylor, who exploded for a league-high 1,811 rushing yards en route to a first-team All-Pro selection. But when the Colts needed to win at least one of their last two games to make the playoffs, Wentz struggled mightily in back-to-back losses to the lowly Las Vegas Raiders and Jaguars. His lackluster performance drew the ire of Irsay.
Why Ballard returned : Irsay placed most of the blame for the Colts' end-of-season collapse on Wentz, not the man who traded premium draft capital to acquire him. The owner blasted Wentz at the league's annual offseason meetings, saying in part, "I think the worst thing you can do is have a mistake and try to keep living with it going forward." One could argue that it was unfair for Ballard to escape Irsay's wrath unscathed, but the owner made it clear through his words and actions that he held Wentz most responsible for his disappointment and wanted the QB gone.
What happened : Irsay was so fed up with Wentz that after just one season, the Colts traded him to the Washington Commanders and replaced him with Matt Ryan via a trade with the Atlanta Falcons. But Ryan, the 2016 league MVP, turned out to be even worse than Wentz as the Colts' offensive line, and ultimately their season, fell apart. Ryan threw 14 TDs against 13 interceptions and was benched. Not long after, Reich was fired midway through the season and replaced by former Colts standout center Jeff Saturday, who had no prior coaching experience in college or the NFL. Indianapolis ended the season losing its last seven games under Saturday, including the worst collapse in NFL history .
Why Ballard returned : If there was ever a time for the Colts to move on from Ballard, this was it. To be clear, it was Irsay's idea to hire Saturday, not Ballard's, but the GM was far from blameless in the team's failures. Ballard admitted in his end-of-season news conference that he'd been "stubborn and dogmatic" in his roster-building approach and even said, "I fired myself 50 times this year." However, perhaps out of loyalty and fondness more than anything else, Irsay didn't fire Ballard. Instead, he gave Ballard another shot and allowed the GM to hire Eagles OC Shane Steichen to be the team's new coach. After that, Ballard turned his attention to one of the most pivotal drafts in franchise history.
What happened : After landing the No. 4 pick, Indianapolis finally bucked its trend of acquiring veteran retread QBs and drafted Anthony Richardson Sr. The dual-threat signal caller showed promise early on, but he only appeared in four games…

full_text:
The Niners and Rams renew their beef for the league's first regular-season game in Australia. Ezra Shaw / Getty Images
The NFL makes its regular-season debut in a faraway land, and picks one of its best possible matchups to mark the occasion.
Super Bowl hopefuls and longtime rivals start their 2026 campaigns together from Melbourne — where McCaffrey glows and Garrett plunders — in the NFL’s first-ever game in Australia . The San Francisco 49ers look to build on their inspired 12-win 2025 season, while the Los Angeles Rams try to make good on their all-in offseason.
In an effort to properly adjust and stave off jet lag, Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers left for Australia more than a week before kickoff. On the other hand, Sean McVay’s Rams arrived in Melbourne about one day before the game.
It’s a blockbuster pairing on all fronts. Here’s what to know about the Netflix national exclusive and over-the-air options for in-market fans.
In Melbourne, kickoff is at 10:35 a.m. local time (AEST) on Friday, Sept. 11.
Noah Eagle, son of fellow broadcaster Ian, has been tapped for the play-by-play call. He is supported by new TV analyst Luke Kuechly, who recently became the second-youngest Pro Football Hall of Fame inductee. Tom Pelissero and MJ Acosta-Ruiz are the sideline reporters.
Elle Duncan anchors the studio show from pregame to postgame. She’s joined by boisterous Hall of Famer Michael Irvin, Super Bowl LII MVP Nick Foles and perennial Pro Bowler Clay Matthews III.
There’s a live performance from the Jonas Brothers, who are set to sing at halftime — rather than the middle of the game itself, which they did during last year’s World Series .
This is the first of five NFL games on Netflix this season. The streamer also has an inaugural Thanksgiving Eve spot, two Christmas specials and a Week 18 flex matchup. Netflix gets the rights to the NFL Honors award presentation during Super Bowl week, too. The full slate looks like this:
While most of the viewership needs a Netflix login to watch Thursday’s game, those in the participating teams’ media markets have an over-the-air simulcast. It’s on NBC Bay Area (KNTV, channel 11) and NBC Los Angeles (KNBC, channel 4).
San Francisco has reached double-digit wins in five of the last seven years. But last season’s 12-5 finish was exceptional, given a cruel stretch of injuries that warped its depth. Unfortunately, the injury misfortune has already started this year. Defensive tackle Alfred Collins tore his patellar tendon at Tuesday’s practice and is now out for the season.
The 49ers’ ground game is again paced by three-down back Christian McCaffrey and left tackle Trent Williams, who has made four All-Pro teams since he joined the franchise in 2020.
Quarterback Brock Purdy gains a much-needed possession target in the decorated Mike Evans, a 12-year veteran with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers who is seeking a second wind on the West Coast. He also reunites with the shifty Deebo Samuel, who is back in San Francisco after his one-year stop with the Washington Commanders. Stalwart tight end George Kittle “ looks good ” for Thursday despite tearing his Achilles tendon during January’s playoff run.
The defense gets a fresh start with the return of its two biggest names. Nick Bosa, the 2022 Defensive Player of the Year, is ready to fly off the edge following his recovery from an ACL tear. Linebacker Fred Warner , a four-time first-team All-Pro, has found renewed purpose in coming back from an ankle injury.
No, Daejon Love won’t be suiting up — he’s an alleged scammer , not a Niner. But vibes are starting off high in San Francisco, and they’ll raise even further with a Week 1 statement.
Los Angeles came up just short in last season’s NFC Championship Game. It now takes on the new season as the sizable Super Bowl favorite .
Cannon-armed Matthew Stafford captained last year’s No. 1 scoring offense on his way to his first NFL MVP award. Puka Nacua led the league in catches and receiving yards per game, while Davante Adams ranked first in receiving touchdowns despite missing three contests. They’re all in place for another go-around. McVay has two powerful rushers in Kyren Williams and Blake Corum, plus a rotating group of tight ends for his beloved 13 personnel sets.
The 2025 defense held its own at No. 10 in points allowed, with a 12-sack season from Byron Young and another seven from Kobie Turner. The 2026 unit looks to be even better with three supernova additions.
First came a trade for Trent McDuffie , the two-time All-Pro cornerback and Super Bowl champ from the Kansas City Chiefs. Then came the blockbuster deal for reigning DPOY and single-season sack king Myles Garrett . As if that weren’t enough, future first-ballot Hall of Famer Aaron Donald decided to come out of retirement and reinforce the Rams’ front line.
Donald won’t be on the field for the opener, but L.A. has plenty of talent to hold things down until he’s ready.
San Francisco holds a 78-71-3 edge in the all-time regular-season series, but Los Angeles has won four of the past five meetings. The two teams are tied 1-1 in the postseason.
Shanahan and McVay, coworkers turned competitors , are facing off as head coaches for the 20th time overall. Shanahan takes an 11-8 lead into Melbourne, though McVay won their only playoff duel — a 13-point fourth-quarter rally in the 2021 NFC Championship Game.
They split their home-and-home series last season. The 49ers stole a Week 5 “Thursday Night Football” game in Inglewood, thanks to Eddy Piñeiro’s overtime field goal and the defense’s heroic stop on fourth-and-1. But the Rams returned with a road spoiler of their own in Week 10, when Stafford threw for 280 yards and four touchdowns at Levi’s Stadium.
Most of The Athletic ’s experts are picking the Rams this week, but it’s not unanimous decision.

title: Inside the Rams' and 49ers' radically different travel strategies for Australia Jonathan Jones, Nate Atkins and more 21
summary:
The Rams and 49ers open their seasons in the NFL's first game in Australia. Will Tullos / The Athletic; Sean Gardner, Ezra Shaw / Getty Images
MELBOURNE, Australia — On Tuesday night, the Los Angeles Rams embarked on one of the most uncommon international journeys the NFL has seen. For the league’s first-ever game in Australia, they decided to spend as little time in Melbourne as possible.
The Rams flew overnight on Tuesday, following their third practice of the week, and arrived Thursday mornin
full_text:
The Rams and 49ers open their seasons in the NFL's first game in Australia. Will Tullos / The Athletic; Sean Gardner, Ezra Shaw / Getty Images
MELBOURNE, Australia — On Tuesday night, the Los Angeles Rams embarked on one of the most uncommon international journeys the NFL has seen. For the league’s first-ever game in Australia, they decided to spend as little time in Melbourne as possible.
The Rams flew overnight on Tuesday, following their third practice of the week, and arrived Thursday morning local time after a 17-hour time change. In 28 hours, they’d be kicking off their season at the Melbourne Cricket Ground. And within two hours of the game ending, they’ll be on another 15-hour flight back to Los Angeles.
They’ll spend about as much time traveling to and from Melbourne as they will in the city itself.
Their approach is the opposite of the San Francisco 49ers’, who are spending close to a week in Melbourne in order to adjust to the local time.
The NFC West rivals received different sets of feedback from their science and research teams, and they realize that, right or wrong, Week 1’s result will give the nation an answer as to which approach was better.
“What gives me confidence is I’m not going to really make it a big deal,” Rams coach Sean McVay said. “It’s, ‘Hey, this is what the reality is. We’ve got a long way to go, but let’s be ready to rock when that three-hour window that we’re allotted comes.’”
The 49ers consulted everyone from sleep experts to coaches who routinely play matches in far-away locales. But really, their approach comes from experience.
“People are probably going to speculate after the game, ‘Well, this was better than the other,’” 49ers offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak said. “But, at the end of the day, we’re going to go out there to play.
“It’s an unprecedented situation. We believe in the way we’re doing it. They believe in the way they’re doing it, and we’re going to play the game.”
The Week 1 affair is the first of a league-record nine international games this season. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell has set his sights on 16 international contests per year, which is likely to coincide with a new CBA that could include an 18th regular-season game to accommodate those hopes.
But before the league gets to 16, it has to get to 10. This spring, NFL team owners voted to have as many as 10 international games beginning in 2027. As recently as 2024, there were just five in a season.
Australia is an important continent to the NFL. There is no language barrier. Explaining the game isn’t overly difficult, considering the country’s background with Australian rules football. It has the money and infrastructure to host NFL games. And it has produced the greatest international player success story to date in Philadelphia Eagles All-Pro offensive tackle Jordan Mailata .
Flag football has been a priority for the league. For the first time, it will be an Olympic sport in 2028, but there’s no guarantee it sticks beyond the Los Angeles Games. With the 2032 Summer Games in Australia, a strong showing by the NFL Thursday night (Friday morning local time) could help flag football’s Olympic future.
You could argue the NFL has proof of concept in Europe. The league has been in London for decades, and countries like Ireland, Spain, France and Germany have hosted or will host games this season. If and when the league awards games to countries like Italy, Austria or Greece, it’s possible the NFL will have a baseline understanding of how those could go.
Australia is a different ball of wax. With its time difference — this is the first NFL regular-season game to be played on a different day local time than in the United States — and long travel, the league needs this game to succeed for the enterprise to be considered worthwhile.
Should the Rams win, the rest of the league might try to copy off their paper. But, at least for now, it’s not something the league is losing sleep over.
“Obviously that’s the club’s choice on when and how they go into the market. I don’t see that as a concern,” said Peter O’Reilly, NFL executive vice president of club business, international and league events. “The fact that a team may be in fewer days in advance of the game, I don’t think does anything to subdue necessarily the energy, the hype, the buzz in a market.
“This offseason, countless numbers of NFL players were in countries around the world doing clinics, connecting with fans around the world. That’s where there’s so much time to create that level of deep engagement with fans around the world. Obviously, it will be interesting to see how this plays out, but I don’t see that as indicative of anything larger or problematic.”
A league source, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, affirmed on background what O’Reilly said publicly last week. “It’s not something that’s on our radar,” the source said.
A high-ranking source at another NFL team, someone with a strong understanding of the league’s international efforts, agreed.
“LA has invested a ton in fan engagement with local artists, media and using alumni and cheer during the week,” the team source said. “I think that’s enough.
Last year, the Rams did something no team ever had. In Week 6, they beat the Ravens 17-3 in Baltimore, with a Week 7 game in London against the Jacksonville Jaguars ahead. Rather than fly back to LA to get a few days of work in, the Rams remained in Baltimore for the entire week of practice.
They flew to London on Friday night and got to town about 30 hours before kickoff to face the Jaguars, who had been there since Monday. The Rams rolled 35-7 against a Jaguars team that would finish the season 13-4. And they weren’t just fresh against Jacksonville — they were arguably at their very best.
The circumstances here aren’t the same, though. Because the Rams spent that week in Baltimore before heading to London, they cut the body-clock change to five hours, compared to 17 with this Melbourne trip. The flight from Baltimore to London was about seven hours, compared to the 15-hour trek the Rams just took to Melbourne, plus a 15-hour trek back.
But that game, along with other successful international journeys, set the template for how the Rams would approach this year’s trip. Soon after they landed the Melbourne assignment in the spring, the franchise was already planning on a last-minute arrival.
They ultimately decided to fly Tuesday night, putting them in Melbourne less than 30 hours before the game. The Rams rented a double-decker Qantas jet with beds for all 53 players. They were advised to stay up two hours later than normal that night. That way, they could keep the body clock the same after an afternoon practice in Melbourne and get a full night of sleep ahead of a 10:30 a.m. kickoff.
“What I think is the most important thing is we make decisions that we feel like are in the players’ best interest, and that’ll guide every approach,” McVay said. “What you have to do is be able to separate the actual result from what is actually sound in terms of your process. I’m comfortable with that. That’s the world that we live in.”
Since coach Kyle Shanahan and general manager John Lynch arrived in 2017, the 49ers have tried to cut back on travel by staying in the Eastern time zone between back-to-back games there and by striving to acclimate to far-flung or unusual venues.
For example, they trained in Colorado Springs ahead of a 2022 game in Mexico City to adjust to playing at altitude. They crushed the Arizona Cardinals, who didn’t practice at altitude, 38-10, only reinforcing their methodical approach. The 49ers will go back to Colorado Springs before a Week 11 game against the Minnesota Vikings in Mexico City this year.
They’ve had similar success on the second leg of back-to-back East Coast games, going 4-1 after training at places such as Youngstown State in Ohio, IMG Academy in Florida and The Greenbrier Resort in West Virginia. Their only loss in that scenario came in Atlanta in 2022…

full_text:
Puka Nacua, Sean McVay and the Rams have owned the NFL offseason. Kirby Lee / Imagn Images; Melina Pizano / Getty Images for LA28
If you are a fan of the Los Angeles Rams, the offseason has been a cross between an unlimited supply of free massages and an endless tube ride at First Point.
In other words, it has resembled something close to ecstasy.
From the trade for one future first-ballot Hall of Fame defensive lineman to the recent unretirement of another , the Rams didn’t merely cement their status as preseason Super Bowl favorites — they practically sent out a call to start planning a parade route for next February.
Only a true cynic could rain on that .
And yet, because I also have my finger on the pulse of the NFL’s 31 other fanbases — and because my L.A. roots don’t preclude me from peering beyond the glitz and glamour — I’m going to take it upon myself to try.
The reality is, if you’re not a fan of the Rams, you’re probably starting to hate them right about now.
To be clear, I’m not saying the Rams deserve your enmity. I’m noting that, over the past seven months, they’ve been a lot .
For some observers, that steady drumbeat toward Super Bowl LXI has become more annoying than Lars Ulrich’s snare on Metallica’s St. Anger album.
When we last saw the Rams in a meaningful football context, they were enduring an NFC Championship Game heartbreak in Seattle to the eventual Super Bowl champion Seahawks, with a discarded franchise icon, Cooper Kupp, adding salt to the sting of a season-ending defeat.
Shortly thereafter, the Rams started winning … and winning … and winning.
The franchise enjoyed a nice moment when quarterback Matthew Stafford, a few days before his 38th birthday, was named the league’s MVP for the first time.
During his acceptance speech at the NFL Honors ceremony, Stafford affirmed that he planned to return for an 18th season, telling his four daughters, who were standing beside him onstage, “I can’t wait for you to cheer me on next year when we’re out there kicking ass.”
From that moment on, the Rams began attacking the offseason — kicking ass and taking names.
In March, L.A. swung a deal with the Kansas City Chiefs to acquire All-Pro cornerback Trent McDuffie, subsequently signing him to a four-year, $124 million contract. Shortly thereafter, another ex-Chiefs cornerback, Jaylen Watson, arrived in free agency via a three-year, $51 million deal.
On the first night of April’s draft, armed with the first-round pick they’d acquired from the Atlanta Falcons the previous year, the Rams surprised everyone and took Alabama quarterback Ty Simpson. By selecting a presumptive QB of the future , general manager Les Snead and coach Sean McVay mitigated any angst among the fan base that their “all-in” approach was overly reckless.
Then came the bombs: In June, L.A. made a blockbuster trade to acquire Cleveland Browns edge rusher Myles Garrett, coming off his second NFL Defensive Player of the Year award in three seasons. The only thing scarier to opposing offenses than trying to block Garrett: Trying to block him and defensive tackle Aaron Donald, a three-time Defensive Player of the Year, who officially came out of retirement on Aug. 30.
Five seasons ago, Donald made the game-clinching play in the Rams’ Super Bowl LVI victory over the Cincinnati Bengals, setting off a wild celebration in their home stadium.
Guess where Super Bowl LXI will take place in February? Yep, SoFi Stadium.
It all seems inevitable, as if Hollywood screenwriters were storyboarding it out over matcha pistachio lattes at Canyon Coffee in Echo Park.
In other words, through no fault of their own, the Rams have created the impression that they’ve taken the suspense — and the fun — out of the 2026 season.
It won’t be that easy, of course, but that hasn’t stopped skeptics from subjecting the Rams to the scrutiny that typically accompanies preordained “superteams.”
This includes judging the behavior of the typically likable McVay, whose draft-night demeanor after selecting Simpson (both in a phone call informing the quarterback of the selection and in a news conference later that night) resembled that of a man in a hostage video.
The coach later explained that he was grumpy for reasons unrelated to the pick, conveying to analyst Chris Simms that a “heated argument about another topic” had preceded the news conference. Various conspiracy theories nonetheless persisted.
In recent weeks, McVay was weirdly cryptic about the Rams’ travel plans for their season-opening game against the San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne, Australia, which will air Thursday night in the U.S. The Rams apparently believe there’s a strategic advantage in sandwiching a pair of long flights (16 hours on the way there, 14 ½ on the return) around a visit to the continent lasting a day and change, which sounds like a buzzkill, but that’s their call.
Declining to reveal their actual itinerary, as McVay did on multiple occasions before finally discussing it this week? That comes off as silly.
Speaking of which, ESPN analyst Dan Orlovsky, Stafford’s former backup with the Detroit Lions, recently said on “Get Up” that if the Rams win another Super Bowl, Stafford enters the conversation as a “top five, top seven” quarterback in NFL history.
With no disrespect to Stafford, who has had a very good career, this is a bit like a former Linkin Park roadie proclaiming that if the band were to come out with another hit album, they’d be considered one of the five best.
One superlative that the 2026 Rams can rightfully claim: Most team captains ever. Like Spinal Tap, they go to 11 , meaning more than a fifth of their active roster will wear jerseys adorned with a “C.”
Somehow, in a division that includes the San Francisco 49ers (Brandon Aiyuk drama, electrical substation intrigue, Kyle Shanahan car accident, Jed York arrest, player-impersonator scandal) and the Seahawks (featured weekly on HBO’s “Hard Knocks”), the Rams are the team some people are sick of hearing about. That’s hard to believe, but it is what it is.
None of this is that serious, but the truth is, Rams haters existed even before this ostentatious offseason. Because of the organization’s aggressive approach to player acquisition and salary-cap manipulation — exemplified by the “F Them Picks” mantra bestowed upon and embraced by Snead — a hearty chorus of naysayers perpetually moans that the Rams will eventually crash out and pay a steep price for their alleged sins.
Further, the trade for Garrett fits right into the larger narrative surrounding L.A.’s professional sports teams and their propensity for landing superstars seemingly at will, sometimes at relatively minimal cost.
Sharing a sports town with the Shohei Ohtani-led Dodgers (coming off back-to-back World Series wins) and the Luka Dončić-gifted Lakers does the Rams no favors when their detractors cast them as entitled.
Some might say the rich get richer. Last week, we learned that an underperforming L.A. franchise — Major League Baseball’s Angels — were being sold by owner Arte Moreno for $4 billion.
The buyer? Rams owner Stan Kroenke, naturally. Expect an announcement any day that the Rams are bringing in Mike Trout as a fantasy football consultant .
It’s Kroenke’s sports world, and the rest of us live in it. He now owns teams in the NFL, MLB, NBA (Denver Nuggets), NHL (Colorado Avalanche), MLS (Colorado Rapids) and the English Premier League (Arsenal).
Kroenke doesn’t own L.A., but if he entered the mayor’s race as a write-in candidate, incumbent Karen Bass and challenger Nithya Raman might be sweating come November.
It seems likely that the winner of that election might be tasked with parade-planning as one of her first official duties. In the meantime, the Rams and their fans are enjoying the ride — even if they’re the only ones who see it that way.

full_text:
Special teams gaffes might have cost the Rams a Super Bowl title in 2025. After churning through special teams coordinators throughout his 10-year tenure, Sean McVay has vowed to fix the problem. Illustration: Dan Goldfarb / The Athletic; Todd Kirkland, Jane Gershovich / Getty Images
This is a story of how two flagship NFL franchises squandered MVP quarterback seasons through a special kind of systemic neglect that could haunt them in the future, Super Bowl expectations be damned.
It might yet become a story of redemption.
The Los Angeles Rams and Green Bay Packers know the agony of flying high with MVP quarterbacks, only to suffer special teams implosions in the biggest games, sabotaging legacies in the process.
Recent trades for superstar pass rushers Myles Garrett (Rams) and Micah Parsons (Packers) distract from a pointed question: What good is adding horsepower to the engine if the radiator empties onto the highway when the car climbs a steep grade?
In January 2022, MVP-to-be Aaron Rodgers watched his top-seeded Packers suffer a blocked field goal and a blocked punt, the latter returned for a San Francisco 49ers touchdown, during a 13-10 playoff loss at Lambeau Field.
In Rodgers’ 2014 MVP season, Seattle burned the Packers for a touchdown on a fake field goal and recovered an onside kick late in the NFC Championship Game. Those plays doomed the Packers on a day Green Bay intercepted Russell Wilson four times.
Last season, Rams MVP-to-be Matthew Stafford suffered a similar fate across three games against the eventual Super Bowl champion Seahawks. The punt-return touchdown his Rams allowed while leading 30-14 in the fourth quarter sparked Seattle to a 38-37 victory in Week 16, costing L.A. the NFC West title and No. 1 seed. In the NFC title game a month later, the Rams muffed a punt, leading to a Seahawks touchdown on the next play as Seattle advanced to the Super Bowl.
These were not isolated failures.
The Rams’ and Packers’ head coaches, Sean McVay and Matt LaFleur, have combined to employ 10 special teams coordinators, including Ben Kotwica’s interim stint with the Rams last season, during otherwise successful tenures. They have new coordinators again entering 2026, along with new hopes. But it’s clear the surface-level treatment of NFL special teams failures — fire the coordinator, hire a new one, act like everything will be fine, then repeat — cannot mask systemic problems.
And so, for the past six months, I’ve asked dozens of special teams coaches, head coaches, coordinators and front-office executives what really matters when analyzing the phase of the game that few truly understand and some head coaches treat as a necessary evil.
Their answers kept returning to decisions made long before kickoff: how much practice and meeting time the head coach commits to special teams, which players claim the final spots on 53-man rosters and which players are active on game day.
These decisions could determine whether McVay’s Rams, among the 10 strongest preseason Super Bowl favorites of the past 15 seasons, deliver on preseason expectations.
It’s late July, and the Rams are finishing practice at Loyola Marymount University when McVay strides over to check out the special teams commitment presentation I’ve prepared after all those conversations dating to the NFL combine.
The presentation begins by framing the Rams’ acquisition of Garrett as a reaction to their meltdowns against Seattle, and watching their division rival win the Super Bowl.
PowerPoint slides show the six special teams coordinators McVay has employed, each stacking over the other, from the venerable John “Bones” Fassel, who let his contract expire so he could coach in Dallas, through the latest hire, Bubba Ventrone.
“I miss him,” McVay says as Fassel’s face flashes onto the screen.
Joe DeCamillis’ face appears. He left the Rams after the 2022 season, taking a job in college because, as he said at the time , “I was just feeling like I wanted to get back with somebody that emphasized special teams.”
“Joe was good, too,” McVay says.
Next comes a look at those three Rams games against Seattle last season. The numbers tell McVay what he already feels. His offense and defense outplayed Seattle by more than three touchdowns (+23.7 expected points), but his special teams gave all of it back (-23.6, the seventh-worst differential out of 1,415 multigame season series this century, per TruMedia).
By this point, McVay has seen stark visual evidence as well: spider charts showing his 2025 team lagging far behind NFL norms in game day roster commitment on special teams, as measured by five categories:
• Core special teamers: Players whose primary role was special teams • Depth ST rate: Rate at which depth spots were used primarily on special teams • Depth ST degree: Degree to which depth players played special teams over offense/defense • Low-use players: Players who were active on game day but played few snaps in any phase • Starter relief: Starters on offense/defense who played regularly on special teams
“We need to f—ing coach and play better, and it needs to be more important to me,” McVay says, “so I agree with everything you are saying.”
The tension reaches into McVay’s football lineage. His grandfather, John McVay, was a 49ers executive during the Bill Walsh years and beyond.
“Who leads the NFL in punt-return average?” Walsh would ask back then. “OK, it’s so-and-so at 13 yards. Who is last in the NFL? OK, it’s so-and-so at 7 yards.”
Walsh would pause for effect and say, “I’ve got a lot of plays that can get 6 yards.”
Great organizations could build dynasties more easily before free agency and the salary cap evened the playing field starting in 1993. There was less need to win in the margins of special teams when Joe Montana was handing off to Roger Craig or throwing to Jerry Rice (those 49ers teams also had Hall of Famers on defense, led by Ronnie Lott).
These are different times, especially with the NFL introducing the “dynamic kickoff” ahead of the 2024 season.
“Special teams wasn’t as important to me as offense and defense,” McVay said, “but now, I think it is more important because there are more action plays. You are covering more kicks, you are returning more kicks, and when the ball is on the 30-yard line, or a touchback goes to the 35, you are really one first down away from being in four-down territory.”
McVay has moved up special teams periods toward the start of practice. That’s progress from August 2025, when McVay’s Rams held a joint practice with the New Orleans Saints and there wasn’t a single special teams period on the schedule.
“Mind-boggling,” a special teams coordinator from an AFC team said. “Like, how is that even a thing?”
McVay and his Saints counterpart, Kellen Moore, built their reputations as offensive play callers. Neither employed established, empowered special teams coaches, who would have pushed back against being marginalized in that way.
The implications reverberated for the Rams, even in less obvious ways. The Saints’ orientation toward offense made it easier for them to trade Rashid Shaheed to the Seahawks at the November deadline. That move, more than any other in-season trade, altered the NFL landscape.
While the Saints were subtracting a one-dimensional speed receiver with modest offensive numbers, the Seahawks were adding a game-changing return specialist. Shaheed’s 58-yard punt return for a touchdown against the Rams in Week 16 helped Seattle take away home-field advantage.
“I told my guys in the special teams room, this play won Seattle the Super Bowl, even though it was a regular-season game,” another special teams coach said. “This changed the course of this game, which gave them home-field advantage in the NFC. That game was over. (The Seahawks) had no morale.”

title: What I’m seeing from the Raiders: Possible life without Bowers, what Maxx Crosby means Plus, a rookie review and ranking the team's 10 best players of training camp and preseason. Sam Warren 8
summary:

HENDERSON, Nev. — “Constant improvement” was a phrase Las Vegas Raiders general manager John Spytek uttered several times during his preseason news conference. It’s what he’s seen from the roster he’s built thus far and what he’s hoping to observe throughout the 2026 season. It is an obvious goal given the troubles of his first season at the helm.
The Raiders went a league-worst 3-14 in 2025.
full_text:
Brock Bowers and Maxx Crosby were the Raiders' two best players this summer. Ethan Miller / Getty Images
HENDERSON, Nev. — “Constant improvement” was a phrase Las Vegas Raiders general manager John Spytek uttered several times during his preseason news conference. It’s what he’s seen from the roster he’s built thus far and what he’s hoping to observe throughout the 2026 season. It is an obvious goal given the troubles of his first season at the helm.
The Raiders went a league-worst 3-14 in 2025. Improvements were made to the coaching staff by bringing in the most sought-after head coaching candidate on the market in Klint Kubiak. Spytek also directed one of the league’s biggest roster overhauls, as just 14 players on this year’s initial 53-man roster predate the general manager’s January 2025 arrival. Only 27 remain from this time last season.
This offseason generated more excitement around the direction of the franchise than there’s been in years — a sense that a return to relevancy is approaching. With the Raiders failing to make the playoffs since 2021, Spytek feels the urgency, saying, “We’ve got to win football games” this year. But he also emphasized the need for patience.
“We’ve been very intentional,” Spytek said. “We’ve talked a lot about that and knowing who we’re bringing into the building. We have a very young roster, which requires development, and development requires time.”
Will such development require another faltering season, or will constant improvement make the Raiders competitive this year? And how are the key pieces in the rebuild fitting in?
Here are some things I’m seeing with the Raiders as they enter the 2026 season.
According to a report from ESPN, star tight end Brock Bowers will miss the start of the regular season after undergoing a meniscus procedure. When asked about Bowers (and Maxx Crosby’s) availability on Wednesday, Kubiak said, “We’re expecting to have all our players ready for Sunday,” though Bowers was officially listed as a DNP on Wednesday’s practice report .
Bowers’ absence would be a massive blow for the Raiders, as he was flourishing in Kubiak’s tight end-heavy system and looked healthy after dealing with a knee injury last season.
Bowers will be the focal point of the offense when he plays. Without him, a major undertaking would be necessary.
The first step in replacing Bowers’ output is getting results from his backups. The Raiders won’t abandon the tight end position in his absence; it’s too much of a factor in Kubiak’s scheme. That means Michael Mayer, Ian Thomas and Connor Heyward will see elevated roles.
Mayer was drafted in the second round in 2023 — two general managers ago. A new regime selected Bowers the next year, relegating Mayer to a complementary role. But Mayer has shown his talents in Kubiak’s scheme during training camp and the preseason, catching four passes for 27 yards and a touchdown over three exhibition games.
“I really love this offense, I really love Klint,” Mayer said during training camp. “It’s just about being comfortable, being the type of player that I can be, and going out there and showing people.”
Mayer can’t do all the things Bowers can — he’s less versatile in his alignment and can’t beat defenders with speed and quickness like the two-time Pro Bowler. But he has the skills and athleticism that won’t force the Raiders to shift things dramatically. He should take on much of Bowers’ receiving opportunities while he’s out.
Thomas served in a blocking role in 2025, his first season with the Raiders. Heyward, a former Steeler, was signed this offseason to be the team’s fullback but can line up at tight end. Neither can come close to replicating Bowers’ ability as a receiver.
That’s why the Raiders will be heavily run-focused without Bowers. Kubiak already utilizes the ground game more than most NFL play callers — the Seattle Seahawks were the third most run-heavy offense in football under his watch last season. That commitment to the ground game helps set up an effective play-action attack.
Without Bowers’ separation ability, the Raiders will need to have success running the ball to create windows for their targets in the passing game. Fortunately for them, running back Ashton Jeanty has returned to practice as a full participant, and rookie Mike Washington Jr. has shown real promise in a supplemental role.
The receivers will also have to step up with Bowers out. Kubiak was critical of them during training camp, saying they’re still looking for a wideout who can help on Sundays. Losing the threat of Bowers puts even more pressure on the group. Given those concerns, look for Kubiak to create space and opportunities for them with his scheme via motions and screens.
Kubiak finally announced Kirk Cousins as the Raiders’ starting quarterback last week, giving him the nod over No. 1 draft pick Fernando Mendoza. They seemingly determined in April, before Cousins was signed, that this would be the approach; both Kubiak and Spytek expressed their preference of playing a veteran ahead of a rookie.
“I think you want to limit the amount of pressure you have on that guy from the start,” Spytek said at the NFL Combine in February. “If you have a young quarterback, I’m not necessarily in favor of running him out there right away either, so another quality player that can play the quarterback position if you have a young quarterback (is important).”
Kubiak has a past relationship with Cousins, who earned two Pro Bowl nominations when they were together with the Minnesota Vikings. Cousins, now 38, looked like he could recapture that form with an impressive showing in training camp and during the preseason.
Cousins commanded Kubiak’s offense throughout offseason practices as he took the majority of first-team reps. The ball seldom touched the ground with Cousins under center — when it did, his enthusiasm and vigor in correcting mistakes resonated with teammates. Kubiak said he’s seen Cousins grow the most in his leadership and control of the offense since their time with the Vikings.
Mendoza showed similar poise in most of his opportunities this summer. He found success throughout practices, connecting with sixth-round rookie receiver Malik Benson for what felt like multiple big plays every day. He embraced the challenge of playing under center after rarely doing so in college, and his snappers said they found no issue with his lack of experience. But he also, understandably, looked new to the NFL at times, testing limits with throws that ultimately led to deflections or interceptions.
The Raiders’ practice play was well represented with preseason performance. Cousins was clinical, going 13-for-17 for 101 yards and a touchdown on his three drives. Mendoza flashed, with a touchdown to Jack Bech and some big throws to Benson and Jalen Nailor, but he also threw two picks, took four sacks and finished with a 55.6 percent completion rate.
Mendoza is the Raiders’ future at the position, and he has the potential to elevate the offense way beyond what Cousins can. But it’s clear that Cousins’ command of the scheme gives them the best chance to win now. Team brass, which has said the best player in the competition will play, owes Cousins the opportunity to provide victories. It also owes its veterans a chance for success.
With Spytek being intentional with development, the situation appears perfect for Mendoza. He’ll watch Cousins operate the offense until it’s decided Mendoza can do better. By then, the hope is Kubiak and Cousins will have laid the groundwork for a winning culture. And in that time, Mendoza will have become steady enough to be depended on.
Here’s how I’d order the Raiders’ top 10 players based on what I saw in training camp and the preseason:
1. TE Brock Bowers: He was the obvious standout of camp. He had explosive receptions or touchdowns in nearly every practice, and looked like the star he proved to be as a rookie. His health is now a concern, but expectations are high when he…

full_text:
Vikings quarterback Kyler Murray enters the 2026 season with a lot to prove and a strong desire to win. Stephen Maturen / Getty Images
When you’ve been in the limelight as long as Kyler Murray has, you live in a state of hyperawareness.
Every action creates a reaction. Every interaction leaves a lasting impression. Every interview gives others a chance to spin words and feelings, shaping a narrative you cannot control.
Murray understands all of this. As a result, he guards against outsiders getting too close. He’s like a fortress. Entering — seeing him for who he really is, deciphering his thought process — feels like standing in front of a vault where only a supersecret code will open it.
Even in a relaxed state, he remains vigilant. Look no further than our conversation last week inside the TCO Performance Center.
At one point, Murray paused in the middle of a revelatory sentence and asked aloud if he should edit himself: “Do I have to keep this PG (rated)?”
He thought carefully. His choice lingered in the air. Then he began again.
“I don’t know, man,” he said. “Calling a spade a spade, I just feel like I’m a real person. There’s no faking it.”
Edited or not, few figures are more interesting in the overarching story of the 2026 NFL season than Murray.
When the Minnesota Vikings signed the veteran quarterback this spring, they introduced hope for a talented roster lacking postseason success under coach Kevin O’Connell. They also lobbed a fascinating unknown into an already ubercompetitive NFC North.
With a Week 1 matchup against the Green Bay Packers approaching, Murray holds the pen in several respects. The 29-year-old can rewrite some of these perceptions trailing him as prominently as numbers on the back of a sports card — such as the notions he’s unserious and self-interested. Murray can also amplify the discussion around how a positive environment affects quarterback performance. He can solidify O’Connell’s status as one of the league’s pre-eminent quarterback maximizers.
Think of Murray what you will, but a closer inspection, featuring insights from former coaches and teammates, reveals far more than any caricature could.
Murray is private, reserved, competitive and loyal. He knows what he wants, and he believes the only way to verify his genuine commitment to football is through achievement.
What is the most fun you’ve ever had playing football?
Murray received the question with a smile.
“Most fun,” he repeated to himself. “Probably high school. Yeah.”
“The innocence of it,” Murray said.
You could see the gears in his brain begin to turn.
“I remember this one afternoon like it was yesterday …”
It was 2014, inside the smelly and sweaty Allen (Texas) High School locker room. Seattle Seahawks safety (and Allen alum) Steven Terrell wove his way to the front of the room for a quick speech in front of the team. Murray listened intently. Terrell talked about the joy of Friday nights. About how much he missed the energy exuding from his teammates and the town.
College, Terrell told them, felt less organic. On an even larger scale, the NFL removed the essence that attracted him to the game in the first place.
But high school football? It distilled all of that down to the most sincere parts of competition and camaraderie.
Murray would come to understand and agree with Terrell’s message.
“Just something about it, man,” Murray said. “I had success in college, and I’ve had some success in the NFL. But high school was just so intimate. It’s never been as intimate as it was then.”
Don’t mistake intimacy for anonymity, either.
Word of Murray’s legend passed through Texas towns like the gospel. Football fans traveled to see the short-statured star, the kid who teleported his way through defenses. Tales were amplified, inspiring more attendees.
Murray’s flair brought a level of buzz familiar to his family.
His father, Kevin, played quarterback at Texas A&M in the 1980s, and newspaper stories from that time depict a college athlete caught in the middle of multiple high-profile sports circumstances. In 1984, the Milwaukee Brewers sued Kevin to keep him from leaving Major League Baseball to play college football. In 1985, a television station alleged Kevin accepted illegal payments to play football at Texas A&M. Some of Kevin’s college coaches suggested exposure from these stories affected the NFL’s evaluation of him several years later.
In this context, trying to shelter Kyler from a similar level of hoopla made sense, and that parenting approach meant building barriers. Those walls made it harder for people to see the younger Murray for who he was. Those who did, such as Allen offensive coordinator Jeff Fleener, understood the public disconnect.
“They didn’t want that attention,” Fleener said. “And because he wouldn’t do a lot of interviews, or he wasn’t answering questions with a certain tone, he was viewed in some ways as a prima donna.”
The ease with which Murray operated on the field, even amid all of the developing noise, didn’t dissuade anyone from those initial impressions.
But it might have masked his foremost trademark: maniacal competitiveness.
Pick anyone in Murray’s life, ask them to describe him with one trait, and they’ll sound scripted.
“He’s a fiery guy,” said Larry Fitzgerald Jr., one of Murray’s earliest teammates in Arizona.
“Outside of Budda Baker,” said former Arizona Cardinals running back Chase Edmonds, “he is the most competitive teammate I’ve had in the locker room.”
“He wants to win so badly,” former Oklahoma coach Lincoln Riley said. “And you feel his competitive nature.”
How long has that been there?
“It’s my whole life,” Murray said. “That’s who I am. I can’t change it about myself. My earliest memories as a family, we’re always competing in something. I always competed in anything I played, whether it was Connect 4, Chutes and Ladders, Candy Land, all of them.”
Years ago, Stephen Baca, Murray’s longtime trainer and close friend, invited Murray to his house to play Sequence.
Baca and his wife dusted Murray, who had never played before.
Before leaving Baca’s house, Murray boxed up the game, held it in his hand and asked: “Can I take this?”
“What do you mean?” Baca responded.
“I want to take this home,” Murray said.
Murray spent the entire night practicing the game and cycling through strategies.
“We were just having fun playing a game,” Baca said. “But he was so pissed that he had to take it, and he still has that box to this day.”
This hunger for winning adds perspective to his animated on-field and sideline interactions with coaches and teammates. Retreating into himself is a way to prevent the emotion from pouring out.
The passion stands out more prominently in this era and at a position that comes with its own set of expectations. Quarterbacks are supposed to carry themselves with even-keeled tact on the field and boisterous traits off it.
Asking Murray to tame his desire is, in a roundabout way, asking him to strip away some of the traits that helped forge his stardom. He grew up in a household with high standards. Anything short of winning was unacceptable.
He has tried to pick his spots more and more. He will continue to try. The same goes for his pledge to divulge more of his true self despite being in a new environment.
After almost every training camp practice this summer, Murray found an unheralded Vikings employee.
He and Dan Ridenour, the team’s head of applied sports science, walked off the field together.
“I think just forming a relationship,” Murray said, as if perplexed by the question. “I’ve been in one place for seven years.”
His experience in Arizona needs no detailed rehashing, but some relationships from that time have persisted.
The Cardinals’ former coach, Jonathan Gannon, said earlier this week he has “nothing but love and respect for K1.” Israel Woolfork, the Cardinals’ quarterbacks coach from 2023 to 2025, described Murray as “misunderstood.” He, too, observed the infamous 2022 independent study clause…

full_text:
Dave Roberts said of Shohei Ohtani's timeline: "I think that now you're talking about two weeks." Jayne Kamin-Oncea / Getty Images
LOS ANGELES — The Los Angeles Dodgers are placing Shohei Ohtani on the injured list, manager Dave Roberts said Wednesday, ending a months-long saga for the hurting four-time MVP and clearing the path for the organization to call up top prospect Josue De Paula directly from Double A.
Ohtani has dealt with nagging knee, biceps and neck issues dating back to at least June, has not pitched since July 3 and has been out of the lineup for the Dodgers in six of their past seven games . The organization struggled with how to handle his growing list of injuries.
“I think that we tried to kick the can as much as we could,” Roberts said, noting that Ohtani’s most pressing issue is his right biceps, which caused him discomfort on a swing during Monday’s game. Ohtani did not disclose the added discomfort until Tuesday night, prompting the Dodgers to nix plans of having him in the lineup Wednesday. Instead, the team pulled the lever on the supremely talented De Paula.
As a two-way player, Ohtani must go on the IL for 15 days rather than 10. He could have his stint backdated to Tuesday, but he won’t be active until the final week of the regular season at the earliest.
“I think that if it were a postseason game tomorrow, he would be in the lineup,” Roberts said. “I think that now you’re talking about two weeks, 14 days. I feel that that’s substantial. He’ll be in a much better place than he was today. Is it going to be 100 percent? Probably not. But I do think that with this time that we’re taking now, he’ll be in an adequate spot to finish the season.”
The Dodgers were reluctant to keep Ohtani out of the lineup even as he has degraded physically. His four-game absence last week was the first time he spent more than two consecutive days out of the lineup since signing with the Dodgers ahead of the 2024 season. It was just the second time Ohtani missed a game because of a physical issue (he missed a May 2024 game in San Diego with lower back tightness).
It took until this week for the Dodgers to acknowledge that Ohtani was unlikely to pitch the rest of the season, a decision that appeared obvious because of the calendar and Ohtani’s regressions in his two attempts to build back up as a pitcher.
This is Ohtani’s first time on the IL since straining his oblique at the end of his tenure with the Los Angeles Angels in 2023.
Despite general manager Brandon Gomes saying last week he didn’t believe Ohtani’s injuries were affecting his offense, the eye test and numbers suggested otherwise. Ohtani was seen shaking out his arm between swings and hobbling off and on for months. He had just six hits in his last 49 at-bats before going on the IL, striking out 21 times in that span. Ohtani’s August was his worst month by OPS (.795) since the opening month of 2022 (.722).
An IL stint has felt overdue. Now, the Dodgers have a needle to thread: getting Ohtani to a spot where he can hold up physically, while having a maximum of only five big-league games to get himself back up to speed before the postseason.
“It’s certainly not ideal,” Roberts said. “I understand that. … But the most important thing is him being as healthy as possible, not compromising his swing, and kind of betting on that.”

full_text:
Cornerback Devon Witherspoon and the Seahawks defense played a role in Drake Maye's subpar performance. Joe Nicholson / Imagn Images
SEATTLE — If it was Drake Maye’s intention to put Super Bowl LX behind him — to look forward to a new season, new challenges, new adventures — he was wildly successful in the New England Patriots’ 2026 opener against the Seattle Seahawks Wednesday night.
For after it was all over — after Maye’s third interception of the game sealed the Seahawks’ 13-10 victory over the Patriots at Lumen Field — who in their right mind would want to talk about New England’s third-year quarterback in anything other than the present tense? In the here and now, using only this Super Bowl rematch as a barometer, it’s not unfair to wonder if Maye is on track to take that heralded “next step” that’s routinely assigned to young athletes who are coming off promising seasons.
All three of Maye’s interceptions took place in the fourth quarter. The last one, the one that’s going to be replayed, rehashed and regurgitated by Pats fans right up to the opening kick of New England’s Week 2 matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers Sept. 20 at Gillette Stadium, wasn’t merely a bad pass. It was the decision-making process that’s at issue, and Maye’s judgment here suggests he was out sick the day they taught the importance of not taking reckless chances on the play before your team has a chance to boot the field goal that could send the game to overtime.
And so it was that on third-and-5 from the Seattle 16, with 26 seconds remaining, Maye looked to his right and threw a pass intended for Mack Hollins. Seattle’s Josh Jobe intercepted it. The pass had a hint of Hail Mary to it, except that it didn’t meet the legal definition of one. Not with Patriots kicker Andy Borregales all warmed up and poised to attempt the field goal that would have kept everyone hanging around to watch the NFL’s much-hyped “Kickoff Game” get decided in overtime.
It wasn’t Maye’s only horrible pass attempt. Earlier in the game, he threw a low ball to new Pats receiver A.J. Brown, and Seattle cornerback Nehemiah Pritchett’s right knee came down on Brown’s right ankle. Brown left the game and did not return . Sure, an extended absence by Brown would have far greater consequences for the Patriots than a season-opening loss, except that’s not the point. Yes, the pass that sent Pritchett’s 190 pounds onto Brown’s ankle was a poorly thrown ball, as Maye himself acknowledged: “I threw one low to him. I should have hit him in the chest.” Maye also under-threw Brown on a flea flicker, though the play drew a pass interference call. (Maye hit rookie tight end Eli Raridon for a two-yard touchdown on the next play.)
There are bad passes … and then there’s trying to win the game on a walk-off TD when there’s a next-play field goal waiting to be kicked. In this situation, a quarterback should have only two targets: His chosen receiver’s midsection or the forehead of a fan in the fifth row of the end zone seats.
Anything in between isn’t just a bad pass. It’s a really, really, really bad idea.
“I lost patience, and it cost us,” Maye said. “They were decisions that cost us the game, on my part, on my end.”
With that response, Maye was talking about the entire mess of a fourth quarter, in which New England squandered a 10-3 lead. Maye hit the trifecta with those interceptions. On the first one, the Seahawks responded with a five-play drive, with a short pass from Drew Lock ( subbing for the injured Sam Darnold ) to Jaxon Smith-Njigba turning into a 45-yard touchdown. On the second one, the Seahawks moved the ball to the New England 8, which was when Jason Myers booted a 26-yard field goal to give Seattle the lead.
And then there was that third interception, which resulted in thousands of very happy Seahawks fans spilling out to the streets of Seattle.
“It was something where we have certain protection on and we’re cutting, and I was trying to get rid of it, realize that Mack was back there in the back,” Maye said. “And I didn’t put enough on it to get it out, and it was just unacceptable.”
Last year’s Patriots were painted as the patron saints of soft schedules. But every season has teams with soft schedules, and most of them don’t get to the Super Bowl. This means the ’25 Patriots shouldn’t be punished for going as far as they did. But take that criticism, and then fold in that Maye and the Patriots were unprepared to play Seattle in the Super Bowl, and it’s easy to make the leap that they wanted to make a statement Wednesday night. If that was their goal, and, specifically, if it was Maye’s goal, then good for all of them. Bulletin-board material will always have a place in competitive sports.
But the time for Maye to make his statement was in overtime. Instead, he threw a pass that not only missed his receiver’s midsection but also missed the forehead of the fan in the fifth row.
Maye had some seven months to get that Super Bowl loss to Seattle out of his head, if indeed he has. This time he only has 11 days to get a season-opening loss to Seattle — and that pass — out of his head. His ascendancy as an elite NFL quarterback depends on it.

full_text:
Patriots quarterback Drake Maye had a tough opening night in Seattle. Jane Gershovich / Getty Images
SEATTLE — Mike Vrabel waited for Drake Maye, hidden beneath the tunnel, out of sight from the fans here celebrating a Seahawks win that arrived swiftly thanks to a shocking interception. The whole scene looked a like February, when Vrabel waited to hug Maye.
Back then, after the Seahawks trounced the Pats in the Super Bowl, Vrabel’s message was simple. They’d barely worked together. Wait until they had a full offseason to tweak things and make additions.
So Vrabel went out and bolstered the roster. He prioritized finding a way to run the ball better and more consistently. He traded for a No. 1 wide receiver. He put faith in the quarterback who finished second in MVP voting a year ago.
And then on Wednesday night, in the Patriots’ first chance to show improvement from the Super Bowl drubbing, the Pats fell flat on their face, giving away a totally winnable game, losing to a backup quarterback, blowing a fourth quarter lead. They lost 13-10 , but this was about more than a three-point loss that might’ve seemed tolerable at the outset of the day.
This was concerning because everywhere the Patriots hoped would be different, so much of what they planned for since February, simply didn’t work.
The running game was supposed to be a new-and-improved unit. It averaged 3.5 yards per carry. The receivers were supposed to give Maye so many better options, but it ended with Romeo Doubs dropping a wide-open pass after A.J. Brown left with an ankle injury that could linger for weeks.
And, most important of all, the Patriots planned to put more on Maye’s plate, hopeful he’d build on an MVP-level season. Instead, he delivered one of the biggest duds of his career, throwing three interceptions, none more costly than the final one when the Pats were already in position to tie the game with a field goal.
“I lost patience and cost us,” Maye said.
In the big picture, there’s still plenty of reason for optimism. This was a brutal first matchup against the defending champs on the road three time zones from home. It was just one night. They lost the opener last year and still went to the Super Bowl.
Still, this season is different. This is the one with massive hope. Expectations for the Patriots are higher than they’ve been since Tom Brady left town.
That’s what happens when you go to the Super Bowl, then revamp the roster and build out a better plan.
And that’s why Wednesday’s loss hurts them even more. All the tweaks they thought would get them past a team like the Seahawks couldn’t even get them a win against Seattle’s backup quarterback.
“We can’t turn the ball over and we have to create more turnovers,” Vrabel said. “It’s a broken record.”
It’s hard to know what the most concerning part is.
Is it a wide receiver group that has been lauded for its depth and is suddenly going to be tested there? Brown could miss multiple games because of this ankle injury. Doubs should be the top guy after him, but his debut was a disaster. His drop preceded Maye’s second interception, and the first one came when targeting Doubs deep. Oh, and two weeks ago they traded Kayshon Boutte, who would have been Brown’s backup.
Is it a running game that was the priority of the offseason, only to come to Seattle and look stuck in the mud, finishing with a success rate of just 22 percent (no team had a success rate last season lower than 30)? Maybe TreVeyon Henderson will help when he gets healthy and maybe this was just a matter of running into a great defense, but that performance stings.
Or is it the quarterback who came out here ready to silence critics who point to his playoff struggles a year ago as evidence that his great regular season was a mirage, only to throw three interceptions and get outplayed by Drew Lock? Surely Maye won’t be that bad the rest of the season. And maybe you can even excuse some aspects of the first two interceptions as a young quarterback getting impatient against a defense that requires you to play the opposite way. But that final interception was unconscionable for a quarterback who is supposed to be one of the best in the NFL.
“Bad football,” Maye called it. “Just unacceptable.”
It is, of course, a long season. Surely there will be Sundays that end with Vrabel hugging players outside the locker room, celebrating great throws from Maye and big plays from Brown.
But Wednesday was supposed to be one of those nights, at least as soon as it became clear the Patriots were left to face Lock instead of Sam Darnold. It was supposed to be a night where the Patriots showed all the ways in which they’ve made progress since the Super Bowl ended.
That progress may arrive later this season and those games in December will matter a whole lot more than this odd Wednesday night kickoff in early September.
But instead, the Patriots fell flat where they were supposed to be most improved. They left Seattle with a completely avoidable loss thanks to some bad football. And none of it felt all that different from the Super Bowl seven months earlier.

full_text:
The Giants hope Jaxson Dart can be the next in a line of quarterbacks to make a Year 2 leap. Al Bello / Getty Images
The hiring of John Harbaugh as coach of the New York Giants has fueled hope that the franchise can experience a rapid turnaround after the 14 dismal seasons that have followed their most recent Super Bowl title. But for all of the optimism generated by the hiring of the Super Bowl-champion coach, second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart will be the most important factor in determining the team’s fate.
Dart’s presence was cited as a driving reason why Harbaugh chose to come to New York over a handful of other opportunities. Dart showed flashes of brilliance as a rookie, demonstrating a playmaking ability possessed only by the best quarterbacks in the league. But those highlights were balanced by plenty of moments when Dart looked like a 22-year-old struggling to figure out complex NFL defenses.
The Giants hope Dart can be the next in a line of quarterbacks to make a Year 2 leap. But it won’t be an easy process, especially as Dart adjusts to a new offense he said in May is asking him to do “a lot of things I haven’t done before.”
“I feel like I’m not even the same person at all,” Dart said Wednesday when assessing his maturation over the past year. “Obviously, the growth you make from the experiences that you have from one year to the next. I just feel like I’ve grown a ton through this offseason.”
Harbaugh oversaw one of the best Year 2 leaps in NFL history while in Baltimore. After making seven starts as a raw rookie in 2018, Lamar Jackson blossomed into an MVP while leading the Ravens to an NFL-best 14-2 record in his second season.
No one is banking on that type of breakout season for Dart. But there is at least a blueprint for the coaching staff to follow as Dart transitions into his second season.
“I think the approach has been similar from the basic idea that we’re trying to build an offense for Jaxson Dart that is amenable to his skill set,” Harbaugh said. “We did the same thing with Lamar. But they’re different people, different quarterbacks — all those kinds of things are different.”
The offensive system the Ravens devised for Jackson was hailed as revolutionary. They blended heavy personnel groupings with Jackson’s singular rushing ability and a passing attack that exploited defenses focused on stopping the run.
Greg Roman, who was promoted to Baltimore’s offensive coordinator in 2019, spearheaded that plan. With Roman designing the rushing attack, the Ravens set an NFL record with 3,296 yards rushing in 2019. The Ravens led the league in rushing again in 2020, and never finished lower than third in Roman’s four seasons as OC. The Ravens moved on from Roman to Todd Monken in 2023 when there was a belief that the offense needed to evolve.
Harbaugh has reunited with Roman, whose title with the Giants is senior offensive assistant, but he’s truly the run game coordinator. Roman has teamed with offensive coordinator Matt Nagy, whose roots are with Andy Reid in Kansas City, and quarterbacks coach Brian Callahan, who is an offshoot of the Sean McVay coaching tree from his time as Bengals OC under Zac Taylor.
This melding of offensive minds has created a system that will challenge Dart to adapt. He essentially ran an NFL version of the Ole Miss offense as a rookie under previous coach Brian Daboll. Leaning on concepts Dart was comfortable with helped Dart enjoy early success, but there is limited upside to such an RPO-heavy offense as defenses evolve. It’s become a trend around the league for teams to pivot to playing their quarterbacks under center more.
That’s been an adjustment for Dart, who operated almost exclusively from the shotgun in college. He was under center on 20.1 percent of his snaps last season, which was the third-lowest rate among quarterbacks with at least 300 dropbacks.
The Giants, who made signing 300-pound fullback Pat Ricard from Baltimore a priority in free agency, are planning to deploy a power rushing attack. The quarterback needs to operate from under center to facilitate that. In turn, the play-action passing game should be opened up.
“The unique thing about this offense is we have strategically built an offense specifically for Jaxson,” backup quarterback Jameis Winston said. “There are a lot of things that allow him to extend plays naturally and just allow him to do his best asset, to see the field. When you have a package where you know everything looks like run, run, run, but we find ways to create explosives out of that, we are at an advantage.”
Dart’s rookie season rarely featured under center play action. Instead, Dart ran the offense while surveying the defense from the shotgun. Under center play action requires the quarterback to turn his back to the defense, which makes reading the defense post-snap more challenging. There’s also a greater emphasis on Dart’s footwork in this system, which must be synced up with the timing of the receivers’ routes.
“When I went back and watched him play last year, it doesn’t always seem like the rhythm and timing of his feet is real intentional based off the routes or concepts they’re running,” said an offensive assistant who was a candidate for a role on the Giants’ staff this offseason and was granted anonymity so he could speak candidly about another team’s player. “It looked like it was just like, ‘I’m going to drop back and find somebody open; I’ll just run around and (hope) … somebody will be open.’”
The transition to the more precise footwork in this system predictably came with growing pains. Callahan called tying Dart’s footwork to his eyes “a constant work in progress” in the spring. Callahan said they had “some very direct conversations” about areas Dart needed to improve and charted out a plan to address those.
“There’s a timing and footwork element to everything in the passing game,” Callahan said during minicamp in June. “If your feet are in rhythm with what the play design is, whether it’s a five-step (drop) or a seven-step or a play-action pass — whatever that timing is for the routes and the route depth with the footwork, is really important. Along with that is where your eyes are. It’s really been an eye discipline and footwork consistency that have been the two things we’ve focused a lot on.”
None of this was a surprise to Dart, who identified his footwork in the pocket as an area he was striving to improve early in the offseason.
“I just think from a footwork standpoint, being able to be cleaner throughout my reads,” Dart said during the first week of OTAs.” There are times when you look back on tape, and maybe you weren’t as quick as you wanted to be through a progression. You look back, and you say, ‘Why was that?’ And it starts with your eyes, making sure they’re in the right spots. And that’s been a huge emphasis with Coach Callahan.”
Dart and the coaches believe he has made considerable progress, but it will be an ongoing process to perfect his footwork. The footwork inconsistency dovetails with another weakness, which was Dart’s sack rate. Despite his athleticism, Dart ranked 29th in sack rate and 28th in pressure-to-sack rate.
“One, he’s too competitive at times. He gets himself out of (trouble) a lot, but it’s the NFL,” ESPN analyst Dan Orlovsky said of the inflated sack rate. “Two, it’s probably still a little bit of (playing) recess football. You’re still playing playmaker, create-a-play football rather than quarterbacking at a consistently high rate.”
Dart has already proven he can hit home runs — think of his scrambling 35-yard touchdown pass to Wan’Dale Robinson to spark the Giants’ 34-17 upset of the Eagles in the quarterback’s third career start.
