full_text:
The Jets need Geno Smith to bounce back after a disappointing 2025. Joe Sargent / Getty Images
What does success look like for the 2026 New York Jets?
It’s a question that’s been posed to anyone associated with this team throughout the summer. For those in the building, the general answer is, simply, competence. There’s not a win or playoff mandate for Aaron Glenn (though it would be difficult to survive another three-win season). This team needs to show a baseline level of competence on both the coaching and player sides, improve significantly on defense (especially with Glenn taking over play-calling), and actually compete from beginning to end.
The 2025 season was an embarrassment. The Jets can’t be an embarrassment again.
Glenn was asked about what success looks like on Tuesday and he said, simply: “Obviously winning. Winning, I mean hands down. Effort, discipline.”
Wide receiver Garrett Wilson was a little more bold when answering the same question: “The playoffs. No doubt about it, man. Nothing else … it’s very realistic. I think it should happen. It’s our job to go play ball and do it. That’s how I feel about it.”
How do the Jets go about meeting those goals — showing improvement across the board, winning more games and, if Wilson is right, making the playoffs?
A lot has to go right. Some things that didn’t happen last year need to happen this year. The Jets’ ability to go on any surprise run to the playoffs (or, frankly, even just appear as part of an “in the hunt” graphic in December) is something of a house of cards. These are likely just some of the things that have to go right for the Jets to achieve their dreams:
By most metrics, Smith was one of the worst starting quarterbacks in the NFL last season. He led the league in interceptions (17) and only won two of his 15 starts. He had a hand in those struggles, but it would also be fair to point out the mess around him: one of the NFL’s worst offensive lines and receiving corps, and a play-calling mess with the offensive coordinator fired midseason.
The Athletic ’s Austin Mock created a new quarterback stat — QB Index — to quantify quarterback performance by factoring in a variety of things. As he writes in the explainer, QBI “strips away the contributions from a quarterback’s 10 offensive teammates and credits only what the quarterback provides on a per-play basis.”
To that end, Smith ranked 32nd of 37 qualifying quarterbacks in QBI last season.
If the Jets are going to find any level of success in 2026, they’ll need Smith to play closer to the 2024 version of himself with the Seahawks, when he ranked 19th of 39 QBs at QBI, per Mock, which drops him into the “average” bucket. That year, Smith passed for 4,320 yards (which would be a Jets record), 21 touchdowns, 15 interceptions and completed 70.4 percent of his passes.
Simply, the Jets need Smith to be average. They haven’t had many seasons with average quarterback play.
Unless Smith is truly terrible or gets injured, the expectation should be that he’ll start all 17 games. The Jets are operating with the belief that Smith can play well enough to come back again in 2027.
This coaching staff loves fourth-round rookie Cade Klubnik, enough that he became the No. 2 quarterback without any serious competition. Klubnik showed some flashes, but there’s also a reason he dropped to the fourth round of last spring’s draft. If the goal is winning games in 2026, the odds of the Jets doing that drop significantly if Klubnik needs to see the field.
We’ve written at length about how good Bailey looked during the preseason and training camp. In our staff’s latest All-32, I predicted he would win Defensive Rookie of the Year. The Jets need the No. 2 pick to live up to that billing.
The Jets’ pass rush is largely reliant on Bailey instantly becoming a productive pass rusher. Neither Joe Ossai nor Kingsley Enagbare have ever topped five sacks in a season. Will McDonald had eight sacks last year, but half of them came in one game against a bad Browns team; he was mostly invisible the rest of the season and again this summer.
As for the other rookies: The Jets drafted three other players in the first two rounds, expecting all of them to make an immediate impact. Wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. will wind up being the primary slot receiver. Tight end Kenyon Sadiq will be used as a unique, versatile weapon. Cornerback D’Angelo Ponds was supposed to compete for a starting job in Week 1 but missed all of training camp with an injury.
It’s probably not realistic to expect all four of them to live up to their billing in one fell swoop — that rarely happens — but if the Jets are going to make some noise, they’ll need this draft class to make an impact like the 2022 class (Wilson, Breece Hall, Jermaine Johnson and Sauce Gardner) did.
Wide receiver Adonai Mitchell and tight end Mason Taylor are two recent second-round picks building plenty of buzz after standout summers. Smith called Mitchell a “special player,” and Glenn has shouted out Taylor as someone he expects to take a leap.
The talent is obvious, but right now it’s all a projection. Neither has produced at the NFL level for a full season yet. Cooper and Sadiq are rookies.
If they all live up to their potential, this could be a fun, explosive offense.
It would be unreasonable for the Jets to expect their offensive line to start all 17 games together again, as they did last year. That’s rare for any unit. But some relative health will be crucial for a group that lacks tremendous depth. Chukwuma Okorafor is an experienced swing tackle but also a significant drop-off if Armand Membou misses any time. The Jets added Jordan Meredith to be a backup center, but he was one of the starters on a bad Raiders offensive line last year (there’s a reason why he was available for a late-round pick swap).
If healthy, this should be a solid offensive line with one potential star (Membou), a couple of quality starters (Joe Tippmann, Olu Fashanu) and a couple stable veterans (Josh Myers, Dylan Parham).
Think about this: A slimmed-down CJ Mosley visited practice this summer, two years since his last NFL game. He retired at 34. Davis is not only thriving at 37, but since he turned 34 he’s played in 83 of a possible 85 games.
Davis was brought in not only for his leadership but also for his ability to handle his business in the middle of the defense. There’s no reason to believe he can’t keep playing at this level, but there isn’t exactly a long history of 37-year-old linebackers thriving either. The hope is that Davis is still a couple years away from a decline.
Sorry if this is controversial, but I would argue that the Jets might need to intercept at least one pass this season. Maybe even more than one.
They certainly need to force more than four turnovers.
Reich’s recent track record isn’t promising. The last time he called plays, in 2023 as the Panthers’ head coach, Carolina ranked 29th in scoring and 30th in yards before Reich was fired midseason. Before the Colts fired him in 2022, Indianapolis ranked 31st in scoring and 27th in yards.
In four combined seasons before that, with better quarterback play, the Colts ranked ninth in scoring and 11th in yards. But that also means Reich hasn’t led a successful NFL offense in five years.
Reich is incorporating new ideas into a playbook built around what he had in Carolina. He’ll also have plenty of help from passing game coordinator Seth Ryan, who is bringing over some concepts from his time under Ben Johnson in Detroit.
The hope is that’s enough to cultivate an offense that ranks better than the bottom-10, as the Jets have in 13 of the last 14 seasons. They have the weapons and offensive line. Do they have the playcaller and quarterback?

full_text:
Without A.J. Brown, the Eagles’ new-look receiving corps aims to take the offense to new heights. Mitchell Leff / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — The Philadelphia Eagles’ locker room looks different.
First, what used to be the back wall, where the offensive linemen sat, has been removed — an extension for the practice squad lockers that used to act like a median in the middle of the room. Less blatant, and more important, were the new placards naming the newly assigned locker stalls.
There was Makai Lemon. A.J. Brown’s “Always Open” sign no longer hung from the stall’s header. Lemon, the No. 20 overall pick, now sits by DeVonta Smith, the most tenured member of an overhauled wide receiver room.
Of course, the locker assignments only further solidify a transition that began months ago . After the Eagles waived Johnny Wilson on Aug. 21, Smith and Darius Cooper officially became the only returning members of Philly’s wide receiver room. Hollywood Brown, Dontayvion Wicks and Elijah Moore — general manager Howie Roseman’s veteran investments — have all moved into a section spanning eight stalls.
Smith is the group’s chosen leader. He once again wears the C on his chest. His only previous selection as a team captain came in 2023. A.J. Brown, a three-time former captain, was the more outspoken of the dynamic duo, which allowed Smith to lean more into his tendency to be a leader seen more often than he was heard.
The Eagles believed Smith could handle more leadership responsibilities long before they traded Brown. Coach Nick Sirianni knew Smith’s actions would back up any further words. Sirianni often points out that Smith is generally the first player at the facility every day. Sirianni sees Smith’s attentiveness in team meetings, his extra work in the weight room on his own time, and his extra work before and after practices.
Smith’s proactive work schedule also serves a familial purpose: He can leave work promptly to be home for his wife , Mya Danielle, and their two young daughters, Kyse and Kali. He stuck to his schedule after Wednesday’s practice. He politely declined to be interviewed, saying he had to be home in time for a special occasion: Kyse had turned 3.
Smith’s approach reflects the togetherness Sirianni emphasized in this season’s first team meeting. The sixth-year coach sees Smith as an example of the culture he wants to build in 2026.
“DeVonta knows that everyone’s success on this team equals team success,” Sirianni said. “And he’s not threatened by anything there because of his position of being just a phenomenal football player, but he’s constantly looking to help people as well.”
Wide receiver coach Aaron Moorehead said he presented the opportunity of being the top dog — as an active leadership role with the other receivers — as “a challenge” to Smith over the offseason.
“He was ready for that,” Moorehead said. “He’s kind of always had that in there, and now it’s just time for him to take that last step of just being The Guy all the time.”
Lemon is Smith’s most sensible protege. The rookie already digested one of his first lessons. They both injured their hamstrings during training camp around the same time, and Lemon, who reinjured the same hamstring he tweaked in OTAs, told reporters he needed to be more “professional” with his preparation. Moorehead said he gave Lemon some pretty straightforward advice: “Whatever Smitty does, you do.”
“And he’s taken to that a little bit,” Moorehead said. “I know that Smitty’s done a good job of going out of his way to help him with some of that stuff.”
Lemon’s availability is essential to the Eagles’ plans for their 2026 passing game. The coaching staff demonstrated this by immediately inserting Lemon into the first-team offense upon his return and playing him throughout the first half of the preseason finale against the Cincinnati Bengals. Even while Lemon was sidelined, Moorehead said the coaching staff “had to come up with creative ways” to simulate the on-field reps Lemon was missing.
Some details were small, but important. Moorehead emphasized how important it was for Lemon to hear quarterback Jalen Hurts dictate the play calls in huddles. Moorehead wanted Lemon to get used to hearing Hurts’ voice — especially with louder environments awaiting in regular-season games. So, Moorehead had Lemon stand in the huddles — as a 12th player — and back away from the action when the others went to run the play.
“It wasn’t the most fun thing in the world,” Moorehead said. “I know he wanted to be out there. We know we all wanted him to be out there. But that’s what you do. You sacrifice your time, you sacrifice your energy to get to where you want to go.”
How ready is Lemon for Week 1? The rookie’s rough debut suggested he may still have a ways to go before he can fulfill the extent of offensive coordinator Sean Mannion’s plan for him in the system. That Sirianni sidestepped a question about Lemon’s readiness by emphasizing his confidence in the entire corps might suggest, at the very least, that Lemon must make use of this week’s practices to further prove that he is indeed ready for a regular-season debut.
“Everybody is in a different spot when you go through an injury,” Sirianni said. “He maybe hasn’t had as many reps. I’m really confident in that room, all the guys in that room, including Makai, and excited about that room and the things that it will bring to our football team. We have a number of different guys that can make plays in that room, and Makai is definitely one of those guys. Looking forward to him having opportunities to be able to do that this Sunday and moving forward.”
Josh Grizzard, Philly’s first-year pass game coordinator, was more effusive in his confidence in Lemon. Grizzard leads many of the wide receiver group’s meetings and sits next to Lemon. Moorehead also sits beside Lemon. Grizzard said Lemon has “done an unbelievable job” of being engaged in meetings and asking strong questions. Grizzard stands near the huddles in practices and watched Lemon learn his alignments and adjustments while sidelined.
“He’s been dialed in,” Grizzard said. “He’s in a good spot, and I know he’s ready to go out there and rock and roll.”
The Eagles are shifting toward more pure progression reads in the passing game, which emphasizes the importance of timing between Hurts and his receivers. Moorehead acknowledged that timing was Lemon’s biggest challenge returning from injury. Moorehead said Lemon has “done a good job” in his return, but said, “like any rookie, (he) is gonna have things that (he’s) gonna do really well, and things that he’s gonna have to improve on.”
The Eagles drafted Lemon partly because the Biletnikoff Award winner was tough to bring down while playing at USC and had a knack for finding room to run. Lemon was the only Big Ten player with more than 500 yards after the catch in 2025 and tied for the FBS lead with 50 first-down receptions. Lemon’s expected usage as a motion receiver aims to create mismatches and opportunities for Hurts to strike Lemon in space.
Yards after the catch stopped being a defining strength of the Eagles’ passing game after the 2022 season. The Eagles’ 4.4 average YAC per reception last season ranked second-lowest in the NFL, per TruMedia. Mannion may not have been using his entire playbook during the preseason. Still, the offense’s reserves averaged a seventh-ranked 5.4 YAC per reception. Can that improvement carry into the regular season with the starters?
If there is any gap in the game plan for Lemon, Moore is next in line. Moore, a six-year veteran, impressed Sirianni by creating explosive plays with straight-line speed on deep balls, jet sweeps, screens and slants. Moore caught two deep touchdowns from Hurts in training camp. But Lemon’s intensity and approach to correcting mistakes encourage the coaching staff.
“It matters (to him),” Moorehead said. “He focuses. He doesn’t want to mess up, and he wants to get in there and make sure — there are 10 other guys…

full_text:
Former Pittsburgh Steelers coach Mike Tomlin (second from right) made his debut in Seattle on Wednesday as NBC's lead NFL studio analyst. NBC Sports
The biggest NFL TV signing of the offseason, NBC’s rookie Mike Tomlin, dropped one of his Tomlinisms almost immediately as he assessed the Super Bowl-winning Seattle Seahawks before their game against the New England Patriots.
Tomlin described how defending champions can be either “hungry or driven.” He then mentioned a “tapeworm.” His overall point was that as the hunted, not the hunter, you have to want it more.
While it was a bit confusing, he could have been detailing his move from Super Bowl-winning Pittsburgh Steelers coach to studio analyst.
Though Tomlin brought much-needed gravitas to the remodeled “Football Night in America” in his regular-season debut, his performance left more of a question than a verdict: To borrow his terminology, does he have a “tapeworm”-like drive for TV or not?
For sure, Tomlin has a lot of potential. His on-air presence is exceptional, as you want to know what he is going to say. He looked pretty comfortable on set and had the signals down on where to look as Maria Taylor quarterbacked a revamped NBC pre-game show that will be on the road every week.
Tomlin was a bit tepid, as it definitely wasn’t fully clear whether this is just a timeout in his coaching career or if he’s going full John Madden, leaving his whistle behind for good for TV. He provided some insight, but it was a little see-no-evil, without a “Wow” moment.
The Seahawks’ injuries on defense? Well, that could be a “blessing in disguise,” Tomlin decided, as Seattle’s head coach Mike McDonald might be inclined to keep the game plans simple and players can be looser. Half-full stuff, for sure.
Tomlin is just 54, even though it feels like he has been around the NFL forever. When Taylor introduced Tomlin at the top of the pregame, she teased that the crew will have to tame Tomlin’s urge to put a coach’s headset on.
It was a warm and appropriate way to bring Tomlin on board. Just like the man he succeeded in Pittsburgh, CBS’ Bill Cowher, Tomlin’s name is probably going to float around every big coaching job that opens. Cowher consistently said no. Will Tomlin?
Tomlin has been high on TV executives’ wish lists for a long time. He received a big contract from NBC that, according to sources with knowledge of his deal but who were not authorized to speak publicly, is a bit back-loaded to entice him to stay longer. NBC clearly wants to build around Taylor and Tomlin.
NBC made a good decision to change its format. Its studio show has consistently been the most-watched on Sundays because it is wedged between the end of the afternoon games and the national spotlight matchup in primetime. It had too many people on the show and cut loose Tony Dungy, Rodney Harrison, Jac Collinsworth and Matthew Berry. A new, improved dynamic was immediately evident: Less is more for each analyst.
Tomlin joined holdovers Taylor, Devin McCourty, Jason Garrett and insider Mike Florio. It felt a little bigger, though the format was irregular for “Football Night in America.” The crew focused on previewing the opening night game, rather than reacting to an afternoon slate of games, like it will the rest of the season.
The show’s best moment belonged to McCourty. After Taylor and Tomlin mimicked shadow boxing following a Seattle segment about building team chemistry, McCourty said how his old Patriots teams used to unwind with some “trasketball,” setting up garbage pail hoops to shoot. But after a late-season loss, Tom Brady cut the basket, saying, “Hey guys, it’s playoff time, let’s focus.”
Tomlin, who was younger than 39-year-old McDonald when he won his Super Bowl with the Steelers in 2009, can take us inside locker rooms and mindsets. How a coach translates that to TV is what breeds success. So while the tapeworm bit had its moments, it needs to be a little better designed to showcase Tomlin’s unique insights.
“I think you learn about yourself,” Tomlin said. “Not only as individuals, but as a collective after you win a world championship. You learn whether or not you are hungry or you’re driven. Certainly, hunger can be satisfied.
“Driven is like a tapeworm. You want to do business when you are in their position with driven people. You need to minimize and eliminate the hungry and really elevate the driven because that’s what it is going to take to answer is some drive, and it’s different being the hunted as opposed to the hunters.”
Throughout the night, Tomlin had a few more quality Tomlinisms, including describing Jaxon Smith-Njigba as “running water,” seemingly to allude to the smoothness of his route running.
To reach the next level, Tomlin will need to reveal hard truths without regard for future jobs.
At halftime, he showed a flash as the NBC crew previewed Thursday night’s San Francisco 49ers vs. Los Angeles Rams game in Melbourne. The 49ers arrived a week or so ago, while the Rams flew in just a day before, taking a completely opposite approach to the time difference. Tomlin was definitely behind San Francisco’s plan.
That is what we need more of from him. It’s probably in him to be a star. How driven is he to succeed on TV? Does he have a tapeworm or not?

full_text:
Joey Porter Jr.'s contract situation is coming up on an important deadline. Barry Reeger / Imagn Images
PITTSBURGH — Flashback to a year ago, when one of the most critical members of the Steelers’ defense was also the most disgruntled. A contract dispute that began with a training camp hold-in remained unresolved for weeks. With the first game of the regular season looming, the player was noncommittal when asked if he’d suit up for Week 1. Finally, on the night before the season-opener, defensive tackle Cameron Heyward agreed to a revised contract.
The names have changed. This year, with just days left until the season opener against the Atlanta Falcons, the Steelers and GM Omar Khan find themselves in the same place with Joey Porter Jr. The talented young cornerback is entering the final year of his rookie contract and is seeking to be part of an ever-growing market at his position. Like Heyward a year ago, Porter also was non-committal recently when asked if he’d play without a new deal.
“Yeah for sure,” he said. “Maybe …”
Taking negotiations down to the wire has become the norm under Khan. It took until the Thursday before the opener in 2021 for T.J. Watt to sign his four-year, $112 million extension. In 2024, Pat Freiermuth didn’t ink his deal until the Friday before the opener.
“I don’t know why,” Heyward said when asked about what appears to be standard practice in Pittsburgh.
“I’d like for everybody to get paid, and I’d like for everybody to be taken care of,” Heyward added. “I’m not going to act like I have every answer to negotiations as a player. Selfishly, I’d like everything to be done so we can focus and just continue to be locked in.”
Deadlines sometimes lead to resolutions and the Steelers drew a hard line many years ago when they decided to never negotiate contracts during the season. That’s a sound policy. The question now, as Khan wades into uncertain waters yet again, is if their tactic of letting contract matters linger — even fester — is working.
“Reward your players earlier and reap the benefits in the long run,” Watt’s brother J.J. wrote on X during T.J.’s latest negotiation in 2025. “Dragging it out not only ends up costing more, it creates unnecessary tension. The longer you wait, the higher the price.”
Watt has a point. A cornerback market that was long overdue for a reset has seen salaries skyrocket this offseason, with four players pushing the ceiling higher almost by the week. After a trade to the Rams, Trent McDuffie became the league’s highest paid-cornerback in March on a deal that pays him $31 million annually. In late July, Cleveland’s Denzel Ward raised the bar to $31.1 million per year. Seattle’s Devon Witherspoon followed on Aug. 15 with a $33 million contract. Finally this week, New England’s Christian Gonzalez became the new highest-paid cornerback at $33.75 million.
Making Porter a top-five paid corner in March, after McDuffie’s deal, would have cost just over $24 million. Now, it would take more than $30 million. Paying Porter like a top-10 player at his position in March would have come with around a $19 million price tag. Now it’s more than $22.5 million. Maybe Porter and his representatives knew this and wanted to let the market grow. But given how often the Steelers have gone down this path, it seems Khan and this front office’s approach is why this is familiar territory.
Take Porter out of this for a moment. Whether you believe he belongs among the top-10 or top-5 highest paid players at his position is not necessarily what this is about. This is more so about the organizational philosophy and approach at the negotiating table. If the Rams, Browns, Seahawks and Patriots avoided these situations, why haven’t the Steelers? And what’s the cost of failing to find a resolution more quickly?
Go back to J.J. Watt’s comments. They were made during the 2025 offseason when T.J. was looking to be the NFL’s highest-paid non-QB. By waiting, the Steelers allowed Myles Garrett to reset the market on a $40 million per year deal that significantly leapfrogged Maxx Crosby’s $35.5 million annual salary. In that situation, the Steelers did have to do exactly what J.J. warned and pay Watt even more on what was, at the time, a record-setting, three-year, $123 million extension.
In addition to the Steelers’ way of doing business, the other thing working against Porter is the franchise-tag system. The team holds considerable leverage because it has the option of asking Porter to play out his deal and then tagging him in 2027 — and even in 2028. Over The Cap currently projects that placing the non-exclusive franchise tag on a corner for the first time in 2027 would cost $23.2 million. That’s a huge difference from the nearly $34 million Gonzalez is making.
“It’s stupid,” Heyward said when asked about the franchise tag. “It hampers players. Why should any team be able to take advantage of a player for one year? It’s used in negotiations.”
As Porter’s contract standoff continues, the outcome could shape how Khan’s first draft class is ultimately measured. On one side of the 2023 class: It’s now fair to call first-round pick Broderick Jones a bust after the team traded him away . On the other side: Keeanu Benton, Nick Herbig, Darnell Washington and Spencer Anderson have proven to be good-value picks from the mid-to-late rounds.
In the middle sits Porter. If the Steelers retain Porter long-term (either with a deal this year or an agreement in the future), Jones looks like the outlier from an otherwise strong class. But if Porter moves on? The Steelers will have failed to retain the 14th and 32nd picks of that draft. In short: Porter represents an important pivot point in how this class should be judged.

full_text:
Dave Roberts said of Shohei Ohtani's timeline: "I think that now you're talking about two weeks." Jayne Kamin-Oncea / Getty Images
LOS ANGELES — The Los Angeles Dodgers are placing Shohei Ohtani on the injured list, manager Dave Roberts said Wednesday, ending a months-long saga for the hurting four-time MVP and clearing the path for the organization to call up top prospect Josue De Paula directly from Double A.
Ohtani has dealt with nagging knee, biceps and neck issues dating back to at least June, has not pitched since July 3 and has been out of the lineup for the Dodgers in six of their past seven games . The organization struggled with how to handle his growing list of injuries.
“I think that we tried to kick the can as much as we could,” Roberts said, noting that Ohtani’s most pressing issue is his right biceps, which caused him discomfort on a swing during Monday’s game. Ohtani did not disclose the added discomfort until Tuesday night, prompting the Dodgers to nix plans of having him in the lineup Wednesday. Instead, the team pulled the lever on the supremely talented De Paula.
As a two-way player, Ohtani must go on the IL for 15 days rather than 10. He could have his stint backdated to Tuesday, but he won’t be active until the final week of the regular season at the earliest.
“I think that if it were a postseason game tomorrow, he would be in the lineup,” Roberts said. “I think that now you’re talking about two weeks, 14 days. I feel that that’s substantial. He’ll be in a much better place than he was today. Is it going to be 100 percent? Probably not. But I do think that with this time that we’re taking now, he’ll be in an adequate spot to finish the season.”
The Dodgers were reluctant to keep Ohtani out of the lineup even as he has degraded physically. His four-game absence last week was the first time he spent more than two consecutive days out of the lineup since signing with the Dodgers ahead of the 2024 season. It was just the second time Ohtani missed a game because of a physical issue (he missed a May 2024 game in San Diego with lower back tightness).
It took until this week for the Dodgers to acknowledge that Ohtani was unlikely to pitch the rest of the season, a decision that appeared obvious because of the calendar and Ohtani’s regressions in his two attempts to build back up as a pitcher.
This is Ohtani’s first time on the IL since straining his oblique at the end of his tenure with the Los Angeles Angels in 2023.
Despite general manager Brandon Gomes saying last week he didn’t believe Ohtani’s injuries were affecting his offense, the eye test and numbers suggested otherwise. Ohtani was seen shaking out his arm between swings and hobbling off and on for months. He had just six hits in his last 49 at-bats before going on the IL, striking out 21 times in that span. Ohtani’s August was his worst month by OPS (.795) since the opening month of 2022 (.722).
An IL stint has felt overdue. Now, the Dodgers have a needle to thread: getting Ohtani to a spot where he can hold up physically, while having a maximum of only five big-league games to get himself back up to speed before the postseason.
“It’s certainly not ideal,” Roberts said. “I understand that. … But the most important thing is him being as healthy as possible, not compromising his swing, and kind of betting on that.”

full_text:
Josh Jobe and Seattle Seahawks celebrate after a game-ending interception in the endzone. Jane Gershovich / Getty Images
SEATTLE — On the fifth play of their reign, trauma intruded. The Seattle Seahawks had barely unveiled their 2025 championship banner when quarterback Sam Darnold started limping. He tried to jog. His right hip protested.
He touched his ailing side. He hopped. He hobbled toward the sideline and then the locker room. Just like that, a team that won the Super Bowl while still ascending heard its first thump of the new season. During a Wednesday night game in a league not known for playing on Wednesdays, the Seahawks found out how hard it is to repeat. The early start to this NFL season yielded the earliest bummer.
Still, they won. They came back from a 10-point deficit that felt like 30 with their offense scuffling. They edged the New England Patriots 13-10 at Lumen Field, torturing the team they pounded in Super Bowl 60 in a different way. The Seahawks were hardy and resourceful. They managed to be the team they’re built to be, even while showing vulnerability without their quarterback.
How good is Darnold? His absence made his value clear.
How good are the Seahawks overall? The rally showcased their championship traits.
How great can they continue to be together? Fingers crossed that the season-opening misfortune doesn’t linger.
As the long night ended, Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald seemed encouraged that Darnold avoided at least one worst-case scenario. Early medical testing ruled out a fracture, he said. But the Seahawks don’t know the extent of his hip injury yet.
“It’s positive, great news,” Macdonald said.
And then: “It’s … uh … let’s say it’s good news right now.”
And soon after: “Our thoughts and prayers are with Sam.”
The man may deserve a PhD in coaching, but don’t call him Dr. Macdonald.
If Darnold can avoid missing significant time — if he can return in a month or less — the Seahawks can survive. Backup quarterback Drew Lock can keep the team competitive. For me, the measure of a quality No. 2 is whether a team can win half its games when he’s the substitute starter. Lock’s task is to play a game simple enough to let Seattle’s all-world defense dictate the rest, but ambitious enough to emphasize the playmaking of wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba.
After being forced into action, Lock was predictably vanilla at the start, but he was exceptional as the game progressed. He completed 16 of 22 passes for 187 yards, with one touchdown and no turnovers. Smith-Njigba, the Offensive Player of the Year last season, put up familiar numbers. He finished with eight receptions for 122 yards, including a 45-yard score on a clever fourth-and-1 play that tied the game early in the fourth quarter.
It was a play that Lock hadn’t run. But he was ready. He’s the football nerd who places a whiteboard next to his bed, just in case he feels the urge to diagram a play. That’s one way he stays sharp despite not playing.
Said Lock: “That’s just kind of been my thing, being able to visualize it so when I read it out, it’s just there in my head.”
It’s always easy to visualize JSN catching a game-changing pass.
“It is, like, a classic football play,” Lock said of the fourth-down deception. “But, no, definitely never ran it. Looked kind of funny before the snap. Didn’t really seem like they had anybody ready to match Jax, based on what I knew we were about to run. He’s actually the third read in that play. When (No.) 11’s  just standing there, you gotta give him the pill.”
But this game wasn’t really about a resilient offense. It was about a Seahawks defense, with a depleted secondary, humiliating New England quarterback Drake Maye once again.
For most of last season, Maye looked like the next top-tier NFL QB. He finished second in MVP voting. He has the size, arm talent and athleticism to lead the next generation of signal callers. Still only 24, he processes the game like a 10-year veteran. To further his growth, the Patriots traded for A.J. Brown, a true No. 1 receiver. Maye is in an ideal situation.
But the last two times we’ve seen him, he has faced a Seattle defensive unit that calls itself the “Dark Side.” The Seahawks defensive line pressures him consistently and mixes in effective blitzes. In a 29-13 Super Bowl blowout, Seattle didn’t relent until the closing minutes. On Wednesday, the Patriots had a better offensive game plan, nibbling at available yards and using the Seahawks’ aggressive style against them. But then came the fourth quarter, and Maye performed like an undrafted rookie just handed the playbook.
Maye threw interceptions to end New England’s final three possessions, each one more horrendous than the last. His final errant toss, a pop fly into the end zone, landed in the mitts of cornerback Josh Jobe. It was a devastating touchback, a mistake from a quarterback whose team was in range to try a game-tying field goal.
“See ball, get ball,” Jobe said afterward of his approach.
Maye, after Brown exited early with an ankle injury, committed turnovers as if he were tossing free T-shirts into the crowd. Darnold spent the night in pain, but he still ended up in better shape than his counterpart.
For the Seahawks, it was fitting that Jobe made the last big play. Earlier in the game, he was fooled on a flea-flicker, and his pass-interference penalty set up the Patriots’ lone touchdown. His game-clinching pick could be considered redemption. Really, though, it’s just the byproduct of the persistence that champions must have.
“The No. 1 thing we have is, we’re just gonna find a way,” said safety Julian Love, one of Wednesday’s stars. “I think the sign of a great team is to be able to win multiple ways.”
The Seahawks’ pregame banner ceremony was not a preview of what comes next. It was a celebration of what happened. Quickly, the game reinforced what they’ve been preaching about the 2026 season. They have to chase their own standard, while the rest of the league chases them. The crown is heavy. The hype about the Los Angeles Rams’ star-studded roster helps ease the burden, but it doesn’t eliminate it. They knew this season would be hard, and then four plays into the journey, the difficulty increased.
But they’re wired to welcome the challenge.
“I think there’s something to be said in the NFL for the expectations you have for yourself,” said wide receiver Cooper Kupp, who has two Super Bowl rings. “Just about everyone on this team has the expectation that we’ll find a way to win, and that goes a long way. There’s power behind that.”
Can the Seahawks still be the Seahawks without Darnold?
For one night, the answer was yes. Barely yes, but still yes.
The new season started with a banner going up, a quarterback going down and a challenger finding a new way to lose to Seattle. Some things about the Seahawks changed with alarming speed. Evidently, badgering the Patriots is not one of them.

full_text:
Backup QB Drew Lock helped the Seahawks overcome a 10-point second-half deficit to beat the Patriots on Wednesday night. Steph Chambers / Getty Images
SEATTLE — Mike McCready, lead guitarist of Seattle-based Pearl Jam, shredded the national anthem to set the stage just minutes before the Seahawks began their Super Bowl title defense Wednesday night at Lumen Field against the New England Patriots.
The Seahawks unveiled the second Super Bowl banner in team history before McCready’s strumming, which drew shades of another Seattle legend, Jimi Hendrix, and his rendition of the Star-Spangled Banner at Woodstock in 1969. Franchise legends like Richard Sherman and Kam Chancellor helped hype up the capacity crowd.
But just five plays into Seattle’s 2026 season, quarterback Sam Darnold was lost for the night because of a hip injury he sustained on a third-down sack by Dre’Mont Jones. Darnold entered the medical tent, then walked slowly to the locker room with a heavy limp on his right side.
“He was going to do everything he can to stay out there,” backup Drew Lock said after the game. “But it was just one of those things where he had to go get it looked at.”
With 57 more minutes to spar with the reigning AFC champion Patriots without Darnold, the Seahawks turned to Lock. He delivered, completing 16 of 22 passes for 187 yards and a touchdown pass as the Seahawks rallied from a 10-point, second-half deficit for a 13-10 win .
Safety Julian Love, who had the second of three fourth-quarter interceptions of Patriots quarterback Drake Maye, was unsurprised.
“We’ve all been saying that Drew has been the best ‘2’ in the NFL for years,” Love said. “It was such a calm on our sideline defensively that folks didn’t even realize until the end of the game, or towards the second half, that he was in.”
Cooper Kupp heaped praise upon Lock, too. The veteran wide receiver said Lock, who draws plays on a whiteboard at home to stay ready, received virtually no reps with the first-team offense during practice this week.
“You can see the onus that he puts on himself to be ready, though, when the time comes,” Kupp said. “There’s extra time he spends on the field, extra time that he spends with the coaches to make sure. The last thing you want is for Sam to have to not be there, but Drew has done an unbelievable job preparing and did a great job for us today.”
Lock held his own in first-year offensive coordinator Brian Fleury ’s inaugural game, save for a few mistakes. He could have easily been picked off on an errant third-down throw in the second quarter. In the third, an illegal shift penalty in the red zone — caused by a late audible with the play clock running down — nullified a would-be touchdown on third-and-4 from the 7.
But Lock also tied the game, with plenty of help from reigning Offensive Player of the Year Jaxon Smith-Njigba. On fourth-and-1 at the New England 45-yard line early in the fourth quarter, Lock faked a handoff, booted left and threaded a short pass through the arms of defensive tackle Milton Williams to Smith-Njigba, who took over from there.
It was a play Lock had never run in practice; on Wednesday, he did so to perfection, getting to Smith-Njigba (the third read in the progression) quickly.
“When 11’s just standing there, you gotta give him the pill,” Lock said with a laugh.
Smith-Njigba immediately evaded safety Craig Woodson, then pulled away and outran pursuit while getting blocks 20-plus yards downfield from tight ends A.J. Barner and Eric Saubert.
“My job was to find the zone, and Drew did a great job of finding me,” Smith-Njigba said. “After that, it was just do what I do, just try to get upfield, protect the ball.”
The play embodied what the Seahawks need Lock to do for however long Darnold is sidelined: Be the point guard of the offense, rather than the playmaker. When Lock was last a full-time starter in 2020 with the Denver Broncos, he went 4-9 in 13 starts.
Two seasons ago with the New York Giants, the No. 42 pick in the 2019 NFL Draft started five games, completing 59.1 percent of his passes with six touchdown passes. But in Denver and New York, Lock struggled with interceptions, including tossing a league-high 15 during the 2020 season and five in 2024.
After the game, coach Mike Macdonald was optimistic about Darnold’s status, saying the team ruled out a fracture, but his prognosis is not yet clear, with more tests to come Monday. The Seahawks’ next game, Sept. 20 at the Arizona Cardinals, could offer Lock his first chance to start since 2024.
Lock said he has grown since he last led an NFL offense as the starter. Much of his improvement, he said, has come from being around a winning franchise like the Seahawks. In turn, his mindset has changed, and Lock has adopted a more conservative approach.
“Knowing the type of defense that we have, there’s no rush to push the ball downfield,” Lock said. “Let’s find ways to get the ball in our guys’ hands. Now when the ones downfield are there, I’ve never been one to be afraid to throw those.
“But having the mindset of taking care of the football, getting it in our guys’ hands, knowing you’ve got the best defense in the world, in my opinion, let’s keep the ball moving forward and see what the scoreboard looks like at the end.”
Though the Seahawks were shut out in the first half, they found a rhythm with Lock at the helm in the second. None of his teammates were surprised, either, nor do they have any doubts about his abilities should the eighth-year pro be called upon to start a few more games.
“Drew came in and did what Drew does every single day at practice,” left guard Grey Zabel said. “I don’t think there was much of a drop-off.”
“I’m super confident in Drew,” added center Jalen Sundell. “Nothing changes when he comes in. Playbook’s the exact same.”
Of course, the plays that Fleury calls could change, just as they did Wednesday. Seattle’s offense, which was already a bit of an unknown entering Wednesday night with Fleury replacing Klint Kubiak, might be a bit more vanilla with Lock under center.
Alternatively, it could get a bit more creative. Third-string quarterback Jalen Milroe, who was used sporadically last season and appeared in three games, could be used in specific packages to take advantage of his running ability.
The Seahawks might also be just fine with Lock, especially with how their defense played Wednesday. Seattle held New England to 277 yards of total offense, and the Patriots’ lone touchdown — scored by tight end Eli Raridon — was made possible by a 34-yard pass-interference penalty on Seahawks cornerback Josh Jobe on a second-quarter flea-flicker.
Jobe got his revenge in the fourth quarter, though, with Seattle’s final interception of Maye in the end zone, sealing the victory with 21 seconds to play.
“It was game on the line,” Jobe said. “Like we talk about, we live in the death zone, and we came alive, and we took the ball away.”
While Seattle’s defense had no issues generating takeaways, its offense avoided them altogether. Sure, the Seahawks finished the evening with just 13 points, which would have tied last year’s team for the fewest in a game. They failed to find the end zone on both of their trips inside the 20.
But with Lock in command and Darnold sidelined, Seattle demonstrated it can play clean football and beat quality opponents like the Patriots.
In the process, Lock made sure Wednesday’s pregame theatrics weren’t all for naught, in as dramatic a prime-time game as any. It was his second comeback victory under the lights at Lumen Field, after he stunned the Philadelphia Eagles with a game-winning TD to Smith-Njigba in 2023.
“I don’t know if my lifespan loves (dramatic prime-time games) as much as I love them in the moment,” Lock said. “But yeah, man, it’s a blast. So proud of everybody helping me tonight on the offensive side of the ball. Can’t say enough about the defense, forcing the turnovers. It was such an awesome night.”

full_text:
The 2026 NFL Melbourne game between the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers will be played at Melbourne Cricket Ground. Kirby Lee / Imagn Images
MELBOURNE, Australia — Getting jet-lagged from all the travel stories?
The San Francisco 49ers’ and Los Angeles Rams’ opposite flight/body clock strategies will be discussed long after kickoff Friday morning (Thursday night in the U.S.), and hey, maybe everyone will start flying luxury airliners and turning right around like the Rams. But let’s focus on the game, which would give the 49ers a serious leg up on the Rams. And that brings us to a big mystery.
How will the teams adapt to the stadium, the historic Melbourne Cricket Ground, which can fit 100,000 people? Particularly, how will the quarterbacks adapt?
The stadium has an oval shape, suitable for cricket and Australian Rules Football but an odd fit for the American version. The 110-meter-long NFL field and goalposts were centered, so fans will be further from the action than in a typical NFL game — and quarterbacks might have a hard time with depth perception and sensing where the sidelines are.
49ers quarterback Brock Purdy is known for layering his passes — teammate George Kittle calls him “Beefy five-layer burrito” — and he is curious what the stadium will feel like as well.
“Obviously it is a big circle, and the field will be in the middle of that circle,” Purdy said. “Having fans sort of further away compared to right up on the sideline — I don’t know if that’ll be a big impact for me or not, but yeah, that’ll be different.”
Locals say the acoustics will be different than a usual NFL game, with delayed amplification from one side of the stadium to the other due to the shape.
Purdy nodded and said he needs to “understand the cadence that we have to be on, the noise and everything, handling that, the operation within the huddle, making sure guys can hear things. I’m sure it’s going to get pretty loud at times, which is cool. Those are fun environments to play in.”
NFL teams don’t have stadium walk-throughs the day before international games; adjustments will happen early Friday morning in Melbourne, where kickoff is at 10:35 local time.
This is the second American football match ever played at the MCG. Maybe the Rams and 49ers will lean on the run game, as the USS Minnesota and the USS Kentucky teams did in 1908.
Other things to watch for:
Former Rams defensive coordinator Raheem Morris said he used to hate going against Deebo Samuel. And now the shoe is on the other foot, as Morris holds the same title with the 49ers and Samuel has returned to the team after a season with the Washington Commanders.
“He’s the ultimate piece that can move around,” Morris said.
The receiver will get carries in the run game against the Rams and is always dangerous on screen passes. The 49ers were lucky that a guy who knew the playbook and is loved by teammates — watch him go from position group to position group before practice — was available in the unemployment line when Ricky Pearsall needed knee surgery early in training camp.
And did we mention Samuel has a chip on his shoulder?
“He’s probably in the best shape since I’ve known him,” left tackle Trent Williams said. “He has always been a dangerous player, but this is the first time he thinks people doubted his ability.”
The 49ers got a break when Rams defensive tackle Aaron Donald decided his comeback can wait until after the 15-hour flights to and from Australia. It does seem the coaching staff backed off a little on pushing fifth-round rookie Carver Willis (who played tackle in college) into the starting lineup, and that perhaps he’d rotate with second-year veteran Connor Colby. Or the 49ers might roll with Colby, who had a rough start to training camp but seemed to be getting most of the first-team work at the three practices here this week.
The 49ers are confident in the four veterans on the rest of the offensive line, but they were a year ago, too. The unit started slow, as the team was 6-4 before winning six of the last seven games.
The 49ers were short-staffed at defensive line even before tackle Alfred Collins suffered a season-ending knee injury Tuesday. Defensive ends Nick Bosa and Romello Height just returned from injuries to practice this week, Mykel Williams is out the first four games and Sam Okuayinono broke his foot last week. Rookie defensive tackle James Thompson Jr. is trying to come back from a hamstring injury and play.
That means the 49ers will likely call up end Ogbo Okoronkwo and tackles Kevin Givens and Sebastian Valdez from the practice squad.
“Unless you guys can name some guys we can fly here real quick,” coach Kyle Shanahan quipped to reporters.
Or unless the 49ers take out a want ad.
“I keep wanting to say rugby, and I know it’s not rugby, but maybe there are some footy guys around here who might be able to do it,” Shanahan said.
On Wednesday, the 49ers worked out Australian rugby player Ben Te Kura , who aspires to become an NFL offensive tackle. He’s previously worked out for the Seahawks and Chicago Bears.

full_text:
Christian McCaffrey (center), Fred Warner (No. 54) and Deebo Samuel (left) have plenty at stake against the Rams in Melbourne. Quinn Rooney / Getty Images
MELBOURNE, Australia — The Los Angeles Rams are like the kid who doesn’t study for the big exam, shows up at the last minute and hopes his natural talent and improvisational skills earn him a passing grade.
And if that happens, it’ll leave his twin, the one who studied for a week, did all his homework and painstakingly made all the necessary preparations, mad as hell.
Welcome, Australian fans, to 49ers versus Rams, which, with all due respect to Jim and John Harbaugh, is the NFL’s biggest sibling rivalry.
The Seattle Seahawks might be the reigning champions of the NFL and the NFC West. They even smoked Super Bowl victory cigars inside San Francisco’s home locker room in February. But the 49ers and Rams aren’t nearly as obsessed with the Seahawks as they are with each other, largely because they’re so similar.
Rams head coach Sean McVay, of course, learned his craft under Kyle Shanahan in Washington. They became head coaches at the same time in 2017; they run the same offense; they compete for the same players; they hire the same assistants. They’re the NFL versions of Cain and Abel.
Which is why their divergent paths to the Southern Hemisphere stand out.
The teams couldn’t have taken more different approaches . While the 49ers arrived one week ago and have done everything the league has wanted — visit coffee shops, attend a footie game, chat up Australian media members and otherwise make NFL inroads in a foreign land — the Rams haven’t done nearly as much.
Their trip amounts to a pop-in. They had a media session and practice yesterday afternoon (Thursday, Melbourne time). They’ll show up for today’s three-hour contest at Melbourne Cricket Ground, then jet back to Los Angeles.
“What gives me confidence is I’m not going to really make it a big deal,” McVay said this week about the team’s approach to the Australia trip. “It’s, ‘Hey, this is what the reality is. We’ve got a long way to go, but let’s be ready to rock when that three-hour window that we’re allotted comes.’”
In that way, a loss might not be such a big deal for the Rams. They didn’t spend much time or many resources on the trip. They didn’t even take Aaron Donald .
Lose to the 49ers and, like the kid who blew off the exam, the Rams can easily explain it away: “Bro, I barely studied! What’d you expect?”
They spent a lot of time and many resources on the trip. They lost a starting player, defensive tackle Alfred Collins, who tore his patellar tendon in Tuesday’s practice . And their show-up-early strategy might put their Week 2 readiness in greater jeopardy, at least compared to Los Angeles.
The Rams’ short turnaround means they’ll never have to adjust to a new time zone. When they return to Southern California, their bodies will still be tuned to Pacific Standard Time. They also play their Week 2 opponent, the New York Giants, on “Monday Night Football,” giving them an extra day to recover.
The 49ers requested that Week 2 Monday game before the NFL schedule came out.
“Yeah, we asked very nicely,” Shanahan said. “Didn’t work.”
The 49ers flew to Australia early to get their bodies onto Melbourne time, a process Shanahan said took time.
“It’s taken me a while to get adjusted here,” he said Wednesday. “I’ve been waking up at one in the morning — wide awake — every day until today. And I was extremely tired before this morning, which I feel is (when I) finally adjusted, which I think is five days.”
He figures it’ll take five days to get back on California time, which the team will have. The 49ers arrive back in San Francisco on Friday afternoon. The first full practice won’t be until Wednesday.
The final layer of this sibling rivalry is that the 49ers are convinced the Rams, the home team in Melbourne, handpicked the 49ers as their opponent to avoid the annual mass migration of 49ers fans to SoFi Stadium. Those games are so packed with red-clad 49ers fans that the Rams often have to use a silent count in their home when their opponent is in town. Moving the game to Australia also turns the 49ers’ shortest annual trip into the longest any NFL team has made in the regular season.
It’s the kind of cheeky move only a brother would make.
NFL teams like to say that intra-division games count double because a victory for one squad also brings a loss for the other. If the 49ers lose to the Rams, it might feel like more than that.

full_text:
The Niners and Rams renew their beef for the league's first regular-season game in Australia. Ezra Shaw / Getty Images
The NFL makes its regular-season debut in a faraway land, and picks one of its best possible matchups to mark the occasion.
Super Bowl hopefuls and longtime rivals start their 2026 campaigns together from Melbourne — where McCaffrey glows and Garrett plunders — in the NFL’s first-ever game in Australia . The San Francisco 49ers look to build on their inspired 12-win 2025 season, while the Los Angeles Rams try to make good on their all-in offseason.
In an effort to properly adjust and stave off jet lag, Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers left for Australia more than a week before kickoff. On the other hand, Sean McVay’s Rams arrived in Melbourne about one day before the game.
It’s a blockbuster pairing on all fronts. Here’s what to know about the Netflix national exclusive and over-the-air options for in-market fans.
In Melbourne, kickoff is at 10:35 a.m. local time (AEST) on Friday, Sept. 11.
Noah Eagle, son of fellow broadcaster Ian, has been tapped for the play-by-play call. He is supported by new TV analyst Luke Kuechly, who recently became the second-youngest Pro Football Hall of Fame inductee. Tom Pelissero and MJ Acosta-Ruiz are the sideline reporters.
Elle Duncan anchors the studio show from pregame to postgame. She’s joined by boisterous Hall of Famer Michael Irvin, Super Bowl LII MVP Nick Foles and perennial Pro Bowler Clay Matthews III.
There’s a live performance from the Jonas Brothers, who are set to sing at halftime — rather than the middle of the game itself, which they did during last year’s World Series .
This is the first of five NFL games on Netflix this season. The streamer also has an inaugural Thanksgiving Eve spot, two Christmas specials and a Week 18 flex matchup. Netflix gets the rights to the NFL Honors award presentation during Super Bowl week, too. The full slate looks like this:
While most of the viewership needs a Netflix login to watch Thursday’s game, those in the participating teams’ media markets have an over-the-air simulcast. It’s on NBC Bay Area (KNTV, channel 11) and NBC Los Angeles (KNBC, channel 4).
San Francisco has reached double-digit wins in five of the last seven years. But last season’s 12-5 finish was exceptional, given a cruel stretch of injuries that warped its depth. Unfortunately, the injury misfortune has already started this year. Defensive tackle Alfred Collins tore his patellar tendon at Tuesday’s practice and is now out for the season.
The 49ers’ ground game is again paced by three-down back Christian McCaffrey and left tackle Trent Williams, who has made four All-Pro teams since he joined the franchise in 2020.
Quarterback Brock Purdy gains a much-needed possession target in the decorated Mike Evans, a 12-year veteran with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers who is seeking a second wind on the West Coast. He also reunites with the shifty Deebo Samuel, who is back in San Francisco after his one-year stop with the Washington Commanders. Stalwart tight end George Kittle “ looks good ” for Thursday despite tearing his Achilles tendon during January’s playoff run.
The defense gets a fresh start with the return of its two biggest names. Nick Bosa, the 2022 Defensive Player of the Year, is ready to fly off the edge following his recovery from an ACL tear. Linebacker Fred Warner , a four-time first-team All-Pro, has found renewed purpose in coming back from an ankle injury.
No, Daejon Love won’t be suiting up — he’s an alleged scammer , not a Niner. But vibes are starting off high in San Francisco, and they’ll raise even further with a Week 1 statement.
Los Angeles came up just short in last season’s NFC Championship Game. It now takes on the new season as the sizable Super Bowl favorite .
Cannon-armed Matthew Stafford captained last year’s No. 1 scoring offense on his way to his first NFL MVP award. Puka Nacua led the league in catches and receiving yards per game, while Davante Adams ranked first in receiving touchdowns despite missing three contests. They’re all in place for another go-around. McVay has two powerful rushers in Kyren Williams and Blake Corum, plus a rotating group of tight ends for his beloved 13 personnel sets.
The 2025 defense held its own at No. 10 in points allowed, with a 12-sack season from Byron Young and another seven from Kobie Turner. The 2026 unit looks to be even better with three supernova additions.
First came a trade for Trent McDuffie , the two-time All-Pro cornerback and Super Bowl champ from the Kansas City Chiefs. Then came the blockbuster deal for reigning DPOY and single-season sack king Myles Garrett . As if that weren’t enough, future first-ballot Hall of Famer Aaron Donald decided to come out of retirement and reinforce the Rams’ front line.
Donald won’t be on the field for the opener, but L.A. has plenty of talent to hold things down until he’s ready.
San Francisco holds a 78-71-3 edge in the all-time regular-season series, but Los Angeles has won four of the past five meetings. The two teams are tied 1-1 in the postseason.
Shanahan and McVay, coworkers turned competitors , are facing off as head coaches for the 20th time overall. Shanahan takes an 11-8 lead into Melbourne, though McVay won their only playoff duel — a 13-point fourth-quarter rally in the 2021 NFC Championship Game.
They split their home-and-home series last season. The 49ers stole a Week 5 “Thursday Night Football” game in Inglewood, thanks to Eddy Piñeiro’s overtime field goal and the defense’s heroic stop on fourth-and-1. But the Rams returned with a road spoiler of their own in Week 10, when Stafford threw for 280 yards and four touchdowns at Levi’s Stadium.
Most of The Athletic ’s experts are picking the Rams this week, but it’s not unanimous decision.

MELBOURNE, Australia — On Tuesday night, the Los Angeles Rams embarked on one of the most uncommon international journeys the NFL has seen. For the league’s first-ever game in Australia, they decided to spend as little time in Melbourne as possible.
The Rams flew overnight on Tuesday, following their third practice of the week, and arrived Thursday mornin
full_text:
The Rams and 49ers open their seasons in the NFL's first game in Australia. Will Tullos / The Athletic; Sean Gardner, Ezra Shaw / Getty Images
MELBOURNE, Australia — On Tuesday night, the Los Angeles Rams embarked on one of the most uncommon international journeys the NFL has seen. For the league’s first-ever game in Australia, they decided to spend as little time in Melbourne as possible.
The Rams flew overnight on Tuesday, following their third practice of the week, and arrived Thursday morning local time after a 17-hour time change. In 28 hours, they’d be kicking off their season at the Melbourne Cricket Ground. And within two hours of the game ending, they’ll be on another 15-hour flight back to Los Angeles.
They’ll spend about as much time traveling to and from Melbourne as they will in the city itself.
Their approach is the opposite of the San Francisco 49ers’, who are spending close to a week in Melbourne in order to adjust to the local time.
The NFC West rivals received different sets of feedback from their science and research teams, and they realize that, right or wrong, Week 1’s result will give the nation an answer as to which approach was better.
“What gives me confidence is I’m not going to really make it a big deal,” Rams coach Sean McVay said. “It’s, ‘Hey, this is what the reality is. We’ve got a long way to go, but let’s be ready to rock when that three-hour window that we’re allotted comes.’”
The 49ers consulted everyone from sleep experts to coaches who routinely play matches in far-away locales. But really, their approach comes from experience.
“People are probably going to speculate after the game, ‘Well, this was better than the other,’” 49ers offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak said. “But, at the end of the day, we’re going to go out there to play.
“It’s an unprecedented situation. We believe in the way we’re doing it. They believe in the way they’re doing it, and we’re going to play the game.”
The Week 1 affair is the first of a league-record nine international games this season. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell has set his sights on 16 international contests per year, which is likely to coincide with a new CBA that could include an 18th regular-season game to accommodate those hopes.
But before the league gets to 16, it has to get to 10. This spring, NFL team owners voted to have as many as 10 international games beginning in 2027. As recently as 2024, there were just five in a season.
Australia is an important continent to the NFL. There is no language barrier. Explaining the game isn’t overly difficult, considering the country’s background with Australian rules football. It has the money and infrastructure to host NFL games. And it has produced the greatest international player success story to date in Philadelphia Eagles All-Pro offensive tackle Jordan Mailata .
Flag football has been a priority for the league. For the first time, it will be an Olympic sport in 2028, but there’s no guarantee it sticks beyond the Los Angeles Games. With the 2032 Summer Games in Australia, a strong showing by the NFL Thursday night (Friday morning local time) could help flag football’s Olympic future.
You could argue the NFL has proof of concept in Europe. The league has been in London for decades, and countries like Ireland, Spain, France and Germany have hosted or will host games this season. If and when the league awards games to countries like Italy, Austria or Greece, it’s possible the NFL will have a baseline understanding of how those could go.
Australia is a different ball of wax. With its time difference — this is the first NFL regular-season game to be played on a different day local time than in the United States — and long travel, the league needs this game to succeed for the enterprise to be considered worthwhile.
Should the Rams win, the rest of the league might try to copy off their paper. But, at least for now, it’s not something the league is losing sleep over.
“Obviously that’s the club’s choice on when and how they go into the market. I don’t see that as a concern,” said Peter O’Reilly, NFL executive vice president of club business, international and league events. “The fact that a team may be in fewer days in advance of the game, I don’t think does anything to subdue necessarily the energy, the hype, the buzz in a market.
“This offseason, countless numbers of NFL players were in countries around the world doing clinics, connecting with fans around the world. That’s where there’s so much time to create that level of deep engagement with fans around the world. Obviously, it will be interesting to see how this plays out, but I don’t see that as indicative of anything larger or problematic.”
A league source, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, affirmed on background what O’Reilly said publicly last week. “It’s not something that’s on our radar,” the source said.
A high-ranking source at another NFL team, someone with a strong understanding of the league’s international efforts, agreed.
“LA has invested a ton in fan engagement with local artists, media and using alumni and cheer during the week,” the team source said. “I think that’s enough.
Last year, the Rams did something no team ever had. In Week 6, they beat the Ravens 17-3 in Baltimore, with a Week 7 game in London against the Jacksonville Jaguars ahead. Rather than fly back to LA to get a few days of work in, the Rams remained in Baltimore for the entire week of practice.
They flew to London on Friday night and got to town about 30 hours before kickoff to face the Jaguars, who had been there since Monday. The Rams rolled 35-7 against a Jaguars team that would finish the season 13-4. And they weren’t just fresh against Jacksonville — they were arguably at their very best.
The circumstances here aren’t the same, though. Because the Rams spent that week in Baltimore before heading to London, they cut the body-clock change to five hours, compared to 17 with this Melbourne trip. The flight from Baltimore to London was about seven hours, compared to the 15-hour trek the Rams just took to Melbourne, plus a 15-hour trek back.
But that game, along with other successful international journeys, set the template for how the Rams would approach this year’s trip. Soon after they landed the Melbourne assignment in the spring, the franchise was already planning on a last-minute arrival.
They ultimately decided to fly Tuesday night, putting them in Melbourne less than 30 hours before the game. The Rams rented a double-decker Qantas jet with beds for all 53 players. They were advised to stay up two hours later than normal that night. That way, they could keep the body clock the same after an afternoon practice in Melbourne and get a full night of sleep ahead of a 10:30 a.m. kickoff.
“What I think is the most important thing is we make decisions that we feel like are in the players’ best interest, and that’ll guide every approach,” McVay said. “What you have to do is be able to separate the actual result from what is actually sound in terms of your process. I’m comfortable with that. That’s the world that we live in.”
Since coach Kyle Shanahan and general manager John Lynch arrived in 2017, the 49ers have tried to cut back on travel by staying in the Eastern time zone between back-to-back games there and by striving to acclimate to far-flung or unusual venues.
For example, they trained in Colorado Springs ahead of a 2022 game in Mexico City to adjust to playing at altitude. They crushed the Arizona Cardinals, who didn’t practice at altitude, 38-10, only reinforcing their methodical approach. The 49ers will go back to Colorado Springs before a Week 11 game against the Minnesota Vikings in Mexico City this year.
They’ve had similar success on the second leg of back-to-back East Coast games, going 4-1 after training at places such as Youngstown State in Ohio, IMG Academy in Florida and The Greenbrier Resort in West Virginia. Their only loss in that scenario came in Atlanta in 2022…

full_text:
First-year offensive coordinator David Blough spent the offseason remodeling the Commanders' system. Scott Taetsch / Getty Images
“Better than a thousand days of diligent study is one day with a great teacher.” — Japanese proverb
ASHBURN, Va. — David Blough is, methodically, swatting at gnats. This is not a metaphor.
It is a late afternoon at the Washington Commanders’ practice facility, where the bugs are feasting. The 31-year-old Blough is, as pleasantly as one can, given the heat and the swarming insects this time of day, discussing — likely for the hundredth time this summer — how he is introducing his football philosophies to the world on the game’s biggest stage as Washington’s first-year offensive coordinator.
A question is posed to him: Who are your teaching influences that aren’t football coaches?
“That’s a great question,” Blough begins. He repeats that phrase after many questions, leaving one to wonder if he actually thinks they are great questions, or just uses that mnemonic to gather his thoughts.
“I’ve listened to a lot of pastors,” he continues. “And some are incredibly gifted, like given the gift of teaching. I grew up in Dallas, right in the Bible Belt. And there was a pastor down there named Matt Chandler, who’s an excellent teacher, as good as I’ve ever heard. There’s a pastor in the church that my wife and I went to (in Plano, Texas) named Jamin Roller . There’s a pastor here in D.C., at McLean Bible Church , named David Platt, and Mike Kelsey, both those guys. So you hear the rhythm with which they speak. You see the different methods with which they communicate, the analogies, the technology they use. You talk about rhythm, right? We have rhythms in meetings; they have rhythms of sermons. And it’s the same thing as if you’re teaching your young men.”
To be sure, professional football is primarily about physical strength and playing to the edge of mayhem — but with purpose and precision. As Washington guard Sam Cosmi puts it, “It’s really hard to mimic (the physicality required for) O-Line. If I did that in public, I’d be behind bars.”
But it’s also about processing data, at an incredibly advanced rate, found within complex ideas. That requires someone who can teach those ideas and terminologies to players who learn in different ways and at different speeds. For the first time in his meteoric rise through the NFL’s coaching ranks, Blough is the primary instructor.
Of all the bets the Commanders are making in this third season under general manager Adam Peters and head coach Dan Quinn, among the biggest is that their two new, first-time coordinators — Blough on offense and Daronte Jones on defense — can teach their systems, rapidly and completely and effectively, to their respective sides of the football, starting Sunday against the Philadelphia Eagles. Nothing much is riding on this, other than the success or failure of a multibillion-dollar franchise, centered around a once-in-a-generation quarterback in Jayden Daniels, and/or the head coach’s job security.
Since the start of OTAs in May, Blough and Jones have put their football philosophies into practice, both individually and through their coaching staffs. But the how matters just as much as the what.
“We spend a lot of time thinking about this,” Blough said. “I didn’t want, we didn’t want, any young man to walk out thinking that they couldn’t exhaust all options to learn. So if they wanted to learn via walk-through, we’ll have somebody available to walk through. If they want to learn via testing, we can give them a test. If they want to learn via (flashcards), we have flashcards. Different coaches do it in different ways. … There’s a lot of new technology available, from annotation screens and group things they can see on their phones. We want to have all of those options available to each player. And we want to be innovative with it, too.”
At Blough’s request, Commanders quarterbacks wore GoPro cameras during OTAs for the first time. Install meetings showed clips from matches during the recent World Cup to demonstrate how players had to perform under the greatest pressure. Another meeting dipped into the recent Netflix documentary about Rafael Nadal — which showed not only his most glorious moments on the court, but the physical suffering he endured to reach those incredible heights.
Both coordinators not only had new position hires, like D.J. Williams, who took over for Blough as Washington’s quarterbacks coach, but were also working with holdovers from the staffs of former coordinators Kliff Kingsbury and Joe Whitt.
Quinn opted to promote Blough rather than potentially lose him to the Detroit Lions, who wanted to interview him for their vacant OC position. There were proven elite offensive voices out there, like former Miami Dolphins coach Mike McDaniel, who’d proven adept at marrying the running game with explosive pass plays. But Quinn went with Blough, whom he’d hired as assistant quarterbacks coach in 2024, then promoted to QB coach late last season after Tavita Pritchard left to become Stanford’s head coach.
“I was very impressed with Daronte and David, their communication with the players,” Quinn said at the end of the preseason. “And that may seem simple, but I’m telling you, it’s not.”
Blough is young for an NFL OC. There are recent precedents, though, of other teams going young at that position — if one is OK with the burden of proof placed upon him by way of such comparisons.
Kyle Shanahan was 28 when the Houston Texans hired him as offensive coordinator in 2008. Josh McDaniels was about to turn 30 when the New England Patriots officially made him OC in 2006. And Sean McVay, of course, is the patron saint of this new church. He was promoted to offensive coordinator in D.C. in 2014 by then-coach Jay Gruden, having not yet turned 28. At 30, the Los Angeles Rams made McVay the youngest head coach in league history.
Like all of them, Blough has gone places in a hurry. Just three years ago, he was finishing an unspectacular pro career as the emergency practice squad quarterback for the Lions. But at every one of his stops as a player, beginning in high school, he showed high aptitude for not only learning, but being able to explain what he’d learned to his teammates.
Blough’s two years with Daniels in the quarterback room provided ample runway for his latest promotion to stick. They get along. But Blough’s changing much of what Daniels has done for most of his career.
Daniels will play primarily under center rather than in shotgun. He will huddle before plays rather than speed to the line as he did in Kingsbury’s no-huddle offense, which will give him less time to adjust calls and blocking assignments as the play clock goes down. Receivers will be in motion a lot more this season than they were the last two. (This was a criticism of Kingsbury’s offense when things went badly last season, but that critique wasn’t leveled much in 2024, when Daniels was the near-unanimous NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year, setting a league record for completion percentage for a qualified rookie quarterback, at 69 percent.)
There weren’t just the pre-snap changes; training camp was filled with “call-its,” non-scripted plays sent to the quarterbacks in real time to try to put maximum stress on the entire unit to perform. Quinn wanted to see mistakes. Theoretically, it will help everyone learn.
Said Blough: “In our society, right, playing it safe is praised. Now, these men don’t play it safe, because they’re the one percent of the one percent of the one percent. But playing it safe is praised, and everybody has an opinion. So what we say in our room is, ‘Winners fail, and losers hide.’ So we challenge them to go fail. And that’s what DQ means when he says let’s put some stress on ’em, see what they can and can’t handle.”
But none of that would matter if Daniels wasn’t on board — not only with the system, but with how it was disseminated.
During OTAs, teaching the new plays and systems…

title: Jeremiyah Love Headlines Loaded Cardinals-Chargers Week 1 Injury Report
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals and Los Angeles Chargers have revealed their first injury reports of Week 1, and at least in the desert, it was a star-studded list headlined by third overall pick Jeremiyah Love.
"We feel good," Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur said of Love, who is looking to bounce back from a high ankle sprain suffered in preseason play. The Cardinals have previously said they're confident in Love playing against Los Angeles.
Full injury list for each team:
LIMITED - RJ Mickens (ankle), Keaton Mitchell (hamstring), Brenan Thompson (hip), Tuli Tuipulotu (hip)
DNP - Deane Leonard (abs), Khalil Mack (rest)
LaFleur was quick to acknowledge how impactful L.A.'s edge room can be.
"Put edge guys on our look squad and add an extra 40 pounds because those guys are heavy, heavy edges, and they play that way," LaFleur said of Mack and Tuipulotu.
"They are hard to move, and when it turns into pass, they know what they're doing. So two solid guys on the edges. ... Both outside linebackers in their spot, they're a problem."
FULL - Blake Gillikin (groin), Will Johnson (ankle)
LIMITED - Jeremiyah Love (ankle), Dadrion Taylor-Demerson, Garrett Williams (Achilles)
DNP - Isaiah Adams (knee), Josh Sweat (rest/knee)
Sweat was confirmed by Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur to be full go ahead of Sunday, so his absence when reporters viewed practice was a bit surprising. Adams and his designation, meanwhile, was a bit expected given his absence within the last few days.
It was good to see all of Williams, Love, Johnson and Back on the practice field, as all were dealing with some sort of injury during preseason.
Williams is making a return from a season-ending Achilles injury in 2025, and LaFleur told reporters his status would be up in the air entering the weekend.
"We want to make sure he feels as good as he can. I think there's a return to play and a return to performance, and you got to lean on the player for that second part," said LaFleur.
"A guy like Garrett, he is as real as they come. So, if he's ready to roll, he'll be ready to roll. And if he needs a little bit more time, then we'll go that way."
Denzel Burke would play in the slot if Williams isn't able to go.
Both the Cardinals and Chargers will practice twice more this week (Thursday and Friday) before placing designations such as out, questionable and doubtful for the weekend.
Saturday, teams are allowed to make up to two standard practice squad elevations. If the Cardinals and Chargers carry questionable or doubtful players into the weekend, pay close attention to what positions each team opts to elevate.
Sunday, 90 minutes prior to game time, the Cardinals and Chargers will reveal their final list of inactives.
Chargers vs Cardinals is set for a 1:25 PM kickoff at SoFi Stadium.
